reqs.text: A complete re-engineering of morm in Rust: define PostgreSQL models in code, track them with rock-solid up and down migrations, and write queries in plain SQL. There is no extra query language. This is a new design, not a port. python-morm is a reference for what real projects need, and nothing is kept just for compatibility.

reqs.text: - `morm-mgr` also runs a migration's Rust data hooks, and nothing else. Build it in CI and ship the binary with the migrations. `migrate --hooks ./morm-mgr` and `rollback --hooks ./morm-mgr` call it as `morm-mgr hook ID up` or `down`, and a migration with hooks refuses to run without it, or if that binary doesn't contain the hook, because `morm-admin` holds no project code. A hook connects with the migration role and runs as a `no-tx` step, so it must be safe to run again on `--resume`.

reqs.text: **How it fits together:** `morm-admin` holds the engine. When a command needs the models, it builds and runs `morm-mgr` to get the manifest. Commands that don't need models (`migrate`, `rollback`, `status`, `purge`) run from `morm-migrations/` alone, so a production host needs `morm-admin` and no Rust toolchain. The app binary carries no migration code or schema metadata, apart from the short per-model column list `check_schema` reads.

reqs.text: **Registration:** models, objects and `sql!` queries register themselves through a distributed static list, with no central list to maintain. Their metadata is behind `cfg(morm_mgr)`, not a cargo feature, because `cargo build --workspace` unifies features and would pull it into the app. `morm-admin` builds `morm-mgr` in its own target directory with that `cfg` set. This needs proof early, including models in several crates, where a linker can drop a crate nothing references (section 16).

reqs.text:
```toml
[database]
# Either a URL, or the separate fields below. Separate fields override URL parts.
url = "${DATABASE_URL}"
host = "/var/run/postgresql"     # Unix socket directory or hostname
port = 5432
name = "app"
user = "app"                     # no password needed with peer auth on a Unix socket
password = "${MORM_DB_PASSWORD}" # keep secrets in the environment
sslmode = "disable"              # disable, prefer, require, verify-ca, verify-full
target_session_attrs = "any"     # "read-write" finds the primary among several hosts
connect_timeout = "5s"
application_name = "auto"        # the binary's name; shows in pg_stat_activity
search_path = "public"           # pinned, so another role can't shadow objects
pooler = "none"                  # "transaction" when connecting through PgBouncer in that mode

[database.migration]             # owner role, so the app can run with fewer privileges
url = "${MORM_MIGRATION_URL}"

[server]                         # optional: the database server, which SQL can't report
ram = "8G"
cores = 4

[pool]
min = "auto"                     # 2 x [server] cores, or of this machine if unset
max = "auto"                     # 10 x min
processes = 1                    # app processes sharing this database
idle_timeout = "5m"              # shrink to 1 after this
last_idle_timeout = "1h"         # then close the last one
max_queries = 50000              # 0 = no limit
max_lifetime = "off"
hold_warn_after = "1h"
wait_timeout = "5s"              # longest wait for a connection; can't be off
max_holds = "auto"               # max / 4, at least 1
lock_timeout = "5s"              # longest wait for one lock
statement_timeout = "off"        # longest single statement
statement_cache = 256            # prepared compile-time statements per connection
shape_cache = 128                # prepared runtime-built statements per connection
shutdown_timeout = "30s"         # db.close() waits this long
plan_cache_mode = "auto"         # or force_custom_plan, force_generic_plan
transaction_timeout = "30s"      # longest db.transaction
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = "1m"
client_connection_check_interval = "5s"
tx_warn_after = "1s"
check_schema = "on"              # "off" starts against a schema that may not match: read the README first

[pools.replica]                  # a read replica
host = "db-replica.internal"
read_only = true

[pools.replica.server]           # a pool on a different server describes that server
ram = "16G"
cores = 8

[pools.jobs]                     # optional named profile
user = "app_jobs"                # any [database] field can be set here
password = "${MORM_JOBS_PASSWORD}"
min = 1
max = 4

[outbox]
batch = 100                      # events claimed at once
poll_interval = "1s"
lease = "60s"                    # a crashed worker's events return after this
max_attempts = 10
retention = "7d"                 # how long delivered events are kept

[telemetry]                      # used by the tracing and metrics features
span_sample = 0.01               # share of queries that get a span: 0 = none, 1 = all
slow_query = "250ms"             # always report slower queries, pool wait included; "off"
metrics_interval = "10s"         # how often metrics are published

[migrations]
dir = "morm-migrations"
min_postgres = 15
scratch_url = "${MORM_SCRATCH_URL}"
```

reqs.text: **`morm-admin import`** is a simple starting point for any existing database. It reads the catalog only, never rows, and writes model files that match the schema exactly: types, nullability, defaults, indexes, constraints and their names. Nothing is "improved". Anything models can't express, such as exclusion constraints or partitioned tables, is listed in its output and stays unmanaged. `morm-admin mgr baseline` then records that state as migration zero. Views, hooks and validation are added by hand afterwards.

use morm::{model, Timestamp};

#[model(
    table = "products",
    base = "common",                 // adds id (identity bigint pk), created_at, updated_at
    ordering = "name, -price",       // default ORDER BY
    was = "items",                   // rename hint: table used to be called "items"
    hooks,                           // this model implements Hooks itself
    extensions = "pg_trgm",
    indexes(
        index(cols = "vendor_id, sku", unique),
        index(cols = "name", using = "gin", ops = "gin_trgm_ops"),
        index(cols = "vendor_id", filter = "deleted_at IS NULL"),
    )
)]
pub struct Product {
    #[col(fk = Vendor::id, on_delete = "cascade", index)]
    pub vendor_id: i64,

    #[col(sql = "varchar(64)", len = "1..=64")]
    pub sku: String,

    #[col(sql = "varchar(255)", was = "title", clean = "trim_name")]
    pub name: String,

    #[col(sql = "numeric(12,2)", default = "0", min = 0)]
    pub price: rust_decimal::Decimal,

    #[col(default = "0", min = 0)]
    pub stock: i32,

    #[col(default = "true")]
    pub active: bool,

    pub attrs: Option<serde_json::Value>,          // jsonb, nullable

    #[col(expr = "price * stock", sql = "numeric")]  // computed in SELECT, not stored
    pub stock_value: rust_decimal::Decimal,

    pub deleted_at: Option<Timestamp>,
}
```

reqs.text: - **An upsert with nothing to update still returns the row.** When the `SET` list is empty, it runs `DO NOTHING`, which writes nothing but returns no row on a conflict, then `SELECT`s by the conflict target, including any `filter`. That's a second round trip only on a conflict. If the row was deleted between the two, the upsert retries once. This path takes no row lock, unlike an upsert with a `SET` list, so inside a transaction use `tx.get_for_update` if you need one. A no-op `SET` was rejected, because it locks the row and writes a new row version on every call.

reqs.text: **Pool deadlocks:**
reqs.block: **R-0446** **Pool deadlocks:**

reqs.text: - **A second connection on the same task is refused.** Using `db` inside a transaction closure, or inside a `stream()` loop, returns `NestedConnection` immediately. This can't be a compile error, because closures can capture `db`. Inside `db.transaction`, morm runs the closure, so a task-local flag works. A `stream()` loop body is ordinary code outside any morm future, so a task-local can't wrap it: an open stream registers its `tokio::task::try_id()` in a small sharded set, and checkout consults that set only while an atomic count of open streams is above zero. A stream registers on its first poll, not at creation, because it's `Send` and can move to another task. Each later poll compares `try_id()` and re-registers if the task changed, which is one integer comparison. An app with no open streams pays one atomic load. The check is per task, so running a stream beside another query in `join!`, `select!` or `FuturesUnordered` is refused too. That really does hold two connections on one task, which is the risk this rule exists for, so such a query uses `db.extra_conn()`. This needs proof early (section 16).

Otherwise a column the app no longer knows about would keep blocking deletes, or cascade them silently. The ledger records each definition. A dropped table moves to the `_morm_retired` schema, with its migration in the name. Long names follow the 63-byte rule with the hash suffix, because Postgres would truncate them and two could collide. The ledger records each original name. Rollback restores them with their data, rebuilds indexes concurrently, and recreates foreign keys and CHECKs as `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE`. Rows changed in the meantime can fail those steps, such as a parent deleted since, or a duplicate where a unique index was, so it stops with the offending rows and offers a decision: clear those values, delete those rows, or keep the constraint `NOT VALID`.

Functions matter because a `BEGIN ATOMIC` body has an empty `prosrc`, so the text search can't see it, but it does record its dependencies. Renaming doesn't break these, which is the danger: a view would keep serving retired data, and the purge would fail later. Dropping a foreign key would quietly remove integrity from a column the app still uses. Retire them together, change them in the same migration, or remove them first. The planner applies managed changes first, so only what still depends after them counts. A generated column's dependency is recorded through `pg_attrdef`, so the query must include it.

reqs.text: - **Code Postgres doesn't track.** A `plpgsql` function body has no recorded dependency on the columns it names, so a retire or rename can break inserts through a trigger like `NEW.note := 'x'`. Before either, morm searches `pg_proc.prosrc` in every schema for the name, whole words only, in any case, because a body in another schema can name the object too, and an unquoted `SELECT N FROM T` names `n` and `t`. Common names like `status` will give false hits, which is fine, because a hit costs a decision, a `plpgsql_check` run and at most a `proof` (steps 35 and 59). A hit on a managed function is a decision with evidence, `makemigrations` proposes the rewritten function, and step 59 proves it with a real call and `plpgsql_check`. `migrate` preflight repeats the search on the live database, which is the only way to see unmanaged functions, and a hit not yet accepted is an open decision, which stops `migrate` with exit code `3` until `--decide` answers it. `rollback` preflight does the same before an inverse that retires or renames. `makemigrations` stores the names to search for in `op_data`, for each direction, because neither command has the models and `rollback` must work from the ledger's `meta.json` when the files are gone.

reqs.text: Static column lists mean a dropped column breaks the old binary mid-deploy. Migrations carry `phase: expand | contract`, and `--phase` splits them. `contract` refuses while a required `#[col(deprecated)]` hasn't shipped. Marking a `NOT NULL` column with no default as `deprecated` generates an expand step dropping that `NOT NULL`, because the new binary stops writing it. A rename decision offers an expand/contract form for live tables: add the new column, keep both in sync with a generated trigger, backfill in batches, and drop the old column and trigger in `contract`. `check_schema` checks compatibility, not equality, at startup, where morm runs it when each pool starts, as R-1116 says, and when `db.check_schema()` is called, so an old binary restarting during an expand phase still boots. Every column the binary reads or writes must exist, with a type the field can decode in the same family as the type it was built against, so only an unrelated kind fails. These are the families, and there are no others: for a field of a Rust integer type, `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint` and `numeric(p,0)` with any `p`, and never a `numeric` with a scale or with no precision, because an integer field has no way to read a fraction; for `Decimal`, `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in its 28 digits; for `morm::Numeric`, `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, as for `Decimal`; for `String`, `text`, and `varchar` with any length or none; for a `String` built against `char(n)`, `char` with any length; for `DateTime<Utc>` and `Timestamp`, `timestamptz` with any precision, and for `NaiveDateTime`, `timestamp` with any precision; and for an array of any of these, an array of its element's family. Every other field needs the same type, with the same length or precision, as `format_type` prints it from `atttypid` and `atttypmod`. `char` is a family of its own, apart from `text` and `varchar`, because Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and a change to `text` or `varchar` drops them, so `'ab '` would read as `'ab'`. Postgres treats those trailing spaces as insignificant, so a `String` field built against `char(n)` reads `char` of any length through a decoder that trims trailing spaces back to `n`: on `char(4)`, `'ab  '` reads as `'ab '`, as it did on `char(3)`, and `'abcd'`, with no spaces to trim, reads whole. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` are different kinds here, because a change between them converts each value through the `TimeZone` of the session that runs it, with no error, so the same stored `12:00` becomes `12:00` UTC under one session and `06:00` UTC under another, and no decoder could tell which. Any other difference fails the check, such as `text` for an integer field, `numeric(25,2)` for an integer field, or `text` or `varchar(3)` for a field built against `char(3)`. Within a family, the check also fails a field built against a type that the column's real type is one of R-1108's silent narrowings of, because Postgres would round or cut what that binary writes with no error: a field built for `numeric(6,2)` on `numeric(4,1)` or on `integer`, for `numeric` on `numeric(6,2)`, for `varchar(3)` on `varchar(2)`, for `text` on `varchar(10)`, for `char(3)` on `char(2)`, for `timestamptz` on `timestamptz(3)`, or for `numeric(6,2)[]` on `numeric(4,1)[]`. It names the column, both definitions and the silent change, such as `1.25` stored as `1.3`. A running binary never meets this, because R-1108 holds such a change for `contract`, which runs once every binary is built for the new shape, or for `--fast`, with apps stopped. So only a binary built for the old shape that starts after it, such as an older build brought back, is refused, and it fails to start loudly, with R-1116's `Error::SchemaMismatch`, rather than storing values other than the ones it writes. A narrowing that raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit still passes, such as a field built for `numeric(6,2)` on `numeric(5,2)` or for `bigint` on `integer`. Within a family, the field reads through the decoder for the column's real type, chosen once per statement when it's prepared, and chosen again when a cached statement is re-prepared because Postgres reports that its result type changed, as it does after a cutover. When the types match, the path is the one the binary always ran. A field wider than the column reads every value losslessly. A field narrower than the column checks each value's range, and only a value that can't fit errors: an integer field returns `Error::OutOfRange` naming the column, never a wrapped value, and `Decimal` returns `Error::Decimal` for a value it can't hold exactly, past its 28 significant digits, as it does on unbounded `numeric`. `morm::Numeric`, and `String` on `text` and `varchar`, read every value whole. Nothing read is rounded. A write goes as the column type the binary was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type, so a value the column can't hold, such as a number with more digits before the point than it allows or a text longer than its length, gets the database's error for that write. Where Postgres would round or cut the write silently instead, R-1108 holds the change for `contract`. So a type change never stops a running binary, and one restarting after it still boots, apart from a binary built for the old shape of one of R-1108's silent narrowings, which the check above refuses. A type change has no expand and contract of its own and never waits for `contract`, apart from R-1108's silent narrowings, and `contract` still guards dropped columns and removed enum values. Extra columns and objects are fine. Two cases that would fail that binary's inserts are reported: an extra `NOT NULL` column with no default, and a column the binary may leave out that is no longer nullable and has lost its default. A column that has lost its identity counts as one that has lost its default, because a binary built while it had one never sends it, so each of its inserts would fail with `NOT NULL`.

reqs.text: morm has no vendor code. It emits OpenTelemetry-shaped data through `tracing` and `metrics`, so Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb and in-house stacks work through exporters the app chooses, and morm depends on no exporter or vendor. reqs.text: - Encode and decode go through one per-column conversion layer, so a column's Rust type can differ from its stored type. Generated code calls `ToSql` and `FromSql` directly through static dispatch, with no pointer or allocation. A field has one decoder for each column type its family accepts, as `check_schema` lists them, and which one a column uses is chosen once per statement from the column's real type when the statement is prepared, never per row. When every column has the type the binary was built against, the statement's rows go through `from_row`, and that path is unchanged: no branch, pointer, allocation or per-row state. Otherwise they go through `from_row_as`, which `#[model]` generates beside `from_row` and which reads each field through the decoder the statement chose. The choice is held by the statement, not the row, so that path adds one branch per value on the statement's choice and no per-row state. `from_row_named` and `ProductRef` work the same way. A parameter is always sent as the column type the binary was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type. A benchmark against hand-written tokio-postgres decoding checks that the unchanged path adds no cost.

Each gives encoding, decoding and `morm::Param`, and a model column uses the Rust type directly, as it does a `PgEnum`. `pg_type` returns `Type::UNKNOWN`, and composite parameters use text format. On its own, `PgDomain`, `PgComposite` or `PgEnum` only binds to a type that already exists: morm doesn't create or change that type. Step 35 adds the attributes that make morm manage one.

reqs.text:
Types are declared once, on their Rust type. A sequence has no Rust type, so it uses a macro:

```rust
#[derive(PgDomain)]
#[pg_domain(name = "email", check = "VALUE LIKE '%@%'")]
pub struct Email(pub String);                       // base type comes from String: text

#[derive(PgComposite)]
#[pg_composite(name = "money_amount")]
pub struct MoneyAmount {
    #[col(sql = "numeric(12,2)")] pub amount: Decimal,
    pub currency: String,
}

#[derive(PgEnum)]
#[pg_enum(name = "order_state")]
pub enum OrderState { Pending, Paid }

morm::pg_sequence!(invoice_no, "START 1000 CACHE 20");
morm::pg_sequence!(order_no, file = "sql/order_no.sql");

Evicting a statement can't, so morm discards the connection, retries once on another outside a transaction, and raises the pool's connection generation. A third error is transient: `XX000` with the message `could not open relation with OID`, from a caller of a `BEGIN ATOMIC` function while a cutover replaces that function or a view under it. It doesn't repeat, and a new statement on the same connection works, so the connection isn't at fault: outside a transaction morm retries once on that connection, held or not, replaces nothing and raises no generation. On a big table that means a long online copy or a table rewrite under a full lock. Adding a value is cheap, but its down is not. morm does all of this safely, but `TextEnum` never needs it.

- **The swap.** Postgres stores an enum value as an internal ID, so moving to a new type always rewrites the data. The one-transaction form is one `tx` step:

1. Set `lock_timeout` and lock every affected table in sorted order, so a busy table fails before anything has changed.
2. Drop column defaults on the affected columns, and anything step 53 drops.
3. For a map that keeps old values, add the retired column and fill it.
4. Rename the old type and create the new one under the real name, with the declared labels.
5. Change each column with `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING`, applying any map, with one `ALTER TABLE` per table so each is rewritten once. The cast fails if a row holds a removed label with no map, which rolls everything back.
6. Copy the owner, comment and grants from the old type, then drop it.
7. Restore defaults and anything step 53 dropped, and check the fingerprint before commit.

`ANALYZE` of each affected table then runs as its own step, because the rewrite removes the column's statistics.

reqs.text: - **Code Postgres doesn't track.** Before any op, or its inverse, that changes a column's type, length or precision, changes a composite type's attributes, drops and recreates a type or view, or renames or removes an enum label, morm walks everything that reaches what changed, of any kind, and repeats until nothing new turns up. This is one rule with no list of kinds, so a kind this text never names is found the same way, and every example here is only an example. The walk starts from what the op reports: each table and column whose type, length or precision changes, each type and view it changes or replaces, including a domain or composite type, and the text of each label that changes. Each round sends everything found so far down two routes. The first is `pg_depend`. It gives every object with a row against something found, and the object something found is part of, which is the target of its row with `deptype` `a` or `i`: a default brings in its column, a check, an index, a policy or a trigger brings in its table, a domain's check brings in its domain, and a view's stored query brings in its view. A break carries on from these: once a table's check calls a found function, whatever writes to that table fails too. From a changed column's own table, rows against that column or against the table as a whole count for any object, and rows against its other columns count for any object R-1102 calls code, because a whole row can carry the changed column while `pg_depend` holds only the column a query names. So a view, a function, a trigger, a policy, a rule, a check, a default or an index that carries code is found on that table whatever column it's on, and a plain index or a foreign key on another column isn't found, and doesn't lead on to anything. From any other table or view found, rows against any of its columns count, because what reads any of it is reached. A trigger also brings in its function, because a row reaches that function whatever it names, and that's the only call the walk follows downward. The second route is the source search. It reads `pg_proc.prosrc`, in every schema but those R-1102 leaves out, for the name of everything found, in whole words, in any case, because a body has no `pg_depend` row for what it names, and a name hits every overload of that name. A `BEGIN ATOMIC` body isn't in `prosrc`, so `pg_depend` gives it instead. An object's name is the word a body writes to use it, such as a function's, an aggregate's, a view's, a table's, a type's or a column's name, or a cast's target type. An operator has no word to match, so its symbol is matched as plain text anywhere in a body, which covers `1 ~~~ 2`, `1~~~2` and `OPERATOR(public.~~~)`, and a longer symbol holding it is a false hit. A name is searched once and an object is found once, so each round can only add to a finite set, and the walk stops at the first round that adds nothing. So it ends whatever shape it meets: a cycle of calls, a function that calls itself, or `pg_depend` rows that lead back to something already found. It has no limit on rounds. On a change to a column's type, length or precision, every function and procedure holding the word `EXECUTE`, by R-1081's search, counts as found from the start, even one that names nothing the change touches, because no tool can see what a built query reads, and whatever calls it is then found by its name. The walk follows objects, not values. A function that a found object only passes the value to as an argument, and that names nothing the change touches, isn't found, such as `pass_f` in `pass_f(max(n))`, because a value can flow through arguments, other tables, application code and other services, further than any tool can follow. That's the walk's stated limit: R-1092's fixed line says it on every widening, and the README says why. The preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse` repeats all of this on the live database, and `makemigrations` stores what the walk starts from in `op_data`, for each direction, because preflight doesn't have the models and `rollback` must work from the ledger's `meta.json` when the files are gone. What counts as a hit is what R-1102 keeps, and everything else found is only walked. A hit on a managed function is a decision, `makemigrations` proposes the rewritten function, and R-1066 and R-1076 prove it. A managed object of another kind that's a hit is a decision too, and it has nothing to call, so the decision is all it gets. After a change to a column's type, length or precision all of these are one decision, as R-1092 says, and after any other op, an enum swap included, each keeps its own. A `plpgsql` body can name a removed label, and a `s::text = 'old'` comparison never fails, it just stops matching.

reqs.text:
- **The steps,** each with its own boundary:

1. `tx`: create the new type under a temporary name.
2. `tx` per table: add the shadow column and a sync trigger on every insert and update, applying the map.
3. `batch` per table: copy by key, with a resumable cursor.
4. `no-tx`: build each index on the shadow column with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for a unique one, named `_morm_new_<name>`, made from the real index's name `<name>` through the 63-byte name function, so step 14 maps a unique violation on it to the field of `<name>`, such as a write of a label the map turns into one another row holds.
5. `tx`, then a separate `tx`: for a `NOT NULL` column add `CHECK (shadow IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`. For a nullable one add `CHECK (<col> IS NULL OR shadow IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, dropped at cutover. Then `VALIDATE`. Any CHECK naming the column goes the same way.
6. `ANALYZE`, because statistics follow the column through a rename.
7. `tx` per materialized view above the column: build it beside the old one on the shadow column, as late as possible, with R-1051's text.
8. `tx`: the cutover, below.

reqs.text: - **The copy walks by key up to a bound,** the highest key read once the sync trigger has committed, and reads that bound and each batch after the trigger has committed. `CREATE TRIGGER` waits for every open write, so any row above the bound was written through the trigger, while a walk that went on until nothing was left chased new inserts for 6,283 batches under nonstop load and finished only when the load stopped, where the bounded copy took 104. A range worked out before the trigger attached misses rows inserted just before it did. `VALIDATE` is the safety net: it fails if any row was missed.

reqs.text: - **The cutover** is one short transaction across all affected tables, and it gives way to live transactions under step 39's rule, with the same settings and the same `--terminate-blockers`, because a waiting lock holds up new readers behind it, and a wait past `deadlock_timeout` lets Postgres kill a transaction. If it can't get in, it stops with nothing changed, and `--resume` carries on from there. It takes each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, dropping anything carried above a view before that view, then locks the tables in sorted order and walks `pg_depend` again, because a reader locks the view first, locking the table first deadlocked every time, and `LOCK TABLE` on a view takes every table under it at once. Sorted order is each table that a foreign key from another affected table references, in name order, then the rest in name order, as step 60's cutover takes the key table first, because readers, and writers going from a parent to its children, lock the parent first, and a cutover that locked the referencing tables first got in on none of 176 attempts under nonstop traffic. It drops the sync trigger, the old indexes and the rest of step 53's dependents, apart from materialized views, renames the old column to a retired column with `NOT NULL` and its default removed, and renames the shadow column to the real name. It sets `NOT NULL` from the validated check, for a column that had it, renames each `_morm_new_<name>` index to `<name>`, re-attaches unique constraints with `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX`, and copies the column's comment and grants. It retires the old type, gives the new type the real name and restores defaults. It swaps each materialized view by rename, under step 39's rules, retiring the old copy, because rebuilding one here would run its query under the lock and break a cutover of milliseconds. Then it recreates the dependents, copies the owner, comment and grants, and refreshes functions.

reqs.text: - **Text on the shadow column.** A partial index, an expression index, a CHECK or a materialized view that names the column takes its text from Postgres by step 39's route. On its throwaway scratch, the new column, the new type and each new object are renamed to their temporary names, and morm reads `pg_get_indexdef`, `pg_get_constraintdef` or `pg_get_viewdef`. So a cast reads the temporary type's name with no text replaced, even when the column and its type share a name. The scratch proof confirms the result: after cutover, each definition must match the one built from the models, and a view whose text differs is checked for the same meaning, as step 39 says.

reqs.text: - **`TextEnum` fallback.** `#[text_enum(unknown)]` on one unit variant works like `#[pg_enum(unknown)]`: any stored value the binary doesn't know decodes to that variant, as one branch on read, instead of returning `Error::UnknownEnumValue`, and writing that variant returns `Error::Validation`. It's opt-in. Without it, an unknown stored value returns `Error::UnknownEnumValue`, with the Rust type's name and the value. This variant has no label: it isn't in the CHECK list, the managed type or `check_schema`, and it can't take `value`, `was` or `deprecated`.

reqs.text: - **Changing a domain or composite type.** A changed domain `check` drops and adds the constraint `NOT VALID`, then runs `VALIDATE` in a separate step. When no column uses a composite type, directly or through an array, a range, a domain or another composite, adding an attribute at the end, dropping the last attribute and changing an attribute's type use `ALTER TYPE`. Any other shape, such as a middle attribute, a new order or a rename, drops and recreates the type in one transaction, keeping its owner, comment and grants. Each of these has an exact inverse. A changed base type, or a change to a composite a column uses, is refused with exit code `2` and changes nothing. Postgres doesn't enforce this: it runs `ADD ATTRIBUTE` and `DROP ATTRIBUTE` on a composite a column uses, and the dropped data is lost. A change that needs a dependent dropped is also refused with exit code `2` and changes nothing: a recreate when anything depends on the type, or `ALTER TYPE` on an attribute a function or view depends on. Step 37 replaces that refusal for managed dependents. `migrate` preflight repeats these checks on the live database, because scratch can't see what no model declares, and `rollback` repeats them before an inverse that drops an attribute. The with-data proof leaves out domain columns whose `check` its rows fail.

reqs.text: **Composite types with dependents.** Step 57 refuses a composite type change that needs a dependent dropped, and the planner replaces that refusal for managed dependents. It walks `pg_depend` from the type, its array type and its attributes, and on through whatever depends on those, and carries functions, procedures, domains, other composite types, and the views, materialized views, triggers and policies above them. In one transaction they're dropped from the outside in, the type is recreated or altered, and they're recreated in the fixed kind order keeping their owner, comment and grants, with an exact inverse. Any other dependent, including one no model declares, stays refused with exit code `2` and changes nothing.

reqs.text: **A view above an online column swap.** R-0566's swap carries a managed view above the column instead of stopping at the retire. Its cutover is one short transaction that gives way to live transactions, as R-1072 says. It takes each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, dropping anything carried above a view before that view, then locks the table and walks `pg_depend` again. A reader locks the view first, so the table comes last, and it never runs `LOCK TABLE` on a view, because that takes every table under the view at once and deadlocked. It drops the sync trigger and any carried objects left, from the outside in, renames the old column to its retired name and the new column to the real name, and recreates the objects from their declarations in the fixed kind order, keeping their owner, comment and grants, so the view reads the new column. Its inverse carries them back the same way. A view no model declares, materialized or not, is refused with the full list before the swap's first step, and `migrate` preflight repeats that. An object the walk can't carry that appears during the copy stops the cutover, which changes nothing: the second walk finds one on the column, and `DROP VIEW`, which never uses `CASCADE`, refuses one on a carried view with `2BP01`. A view that would still read the retired column once recreated, materialized or not, such as `SELECT *`, is refused the same way, which the scratch proof finds in `pg_depend`. A materialized view anywhere above the column follows R-1063. `--fast` still handles all of these in one transaction.

reqs.text: - **Retired materialized views.** An online column swap (step 39) retires the old copy of a materialized view, because a view can hold rows its table no longer has, and one may be frozen on purpose. It moves to the `_morm_retired` schema, named with its migration and following the 63-byte rule, and keeps its rows, indexes, owner, comment and grants. The ledger records its original name. A view or `BEGIN ATOMIC` function it still reads is retired with it, the same way. `verify` doesn't report any of these as drift, and a later op's `pg_depend` walk passes over them. The old copy still reads the retired column, and it's an object being retired under R-0571, so it doesn't stop the swap. `purge` drops the copies from the outside in, then what they read, then the retired columns and type, without `CASCADE`, stopping with the list if anything else depends on them. `rollback`, and `revert` of the swap, drop the new one and move the old one back to its schema and name in the inverse's short transaction, exactly as it was: the same rows, unpopulated if it was, and with no refresh. After `purge`, R-0575 applies. A later change Postgres refuses under a retired copy, such as `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` on another column it reads, is refused with exit code `2`, naming it, and `purge --now` clears it.

reqs.text: **A materialized view above an online column swap.** Recreating one would run its query under the table's lock, so it's built beside the old one. After the copy, `VALIDATE` and `ANALYZE`, as late as possible before the cutover, a step of its own creates it under a temporary name on the shadow column, using R-1064's query, with its indexes, owner, comment and grants, and runs `ANALYZE`. Reads and writes carry on during the build. A view, materialized view or `BEGIN ATOMIC` function between it and the column is built beside it in the same way, innermost first. The cutover swaps each one by rename: the old one is retired, as step 38 says, and the new one and its indexes take the real names. `LOCK TABLE` refuses a materialized view, so the rename takes its lock, from the outside in, before the table's. A view, function or other object above it would stay on the old copy, so R-1061 carries it in the same cutover, recreating it on the new one, and a view no model declares is refused. A rebuild opens a decision naming the view: its contents will come from today's table, and the old copy stays until `purge`, because a view can hold rows the table no longer has, and one may be frozen on purpose. One created `WITH NO DATA` holds nothing, so it's built `WITH NO DATA`, stays unpopulated and opens no decision. `--resume` drops an unfinished build and builds again, so the new copy stays as late as possible, and `rollback --failed` drops it and leaves the old one in place.

reqs.text: - **Managed functions are proven by a real call.** Every managed function or procedure R-1038 finds, and every one step 38's source search finds before a retire or a rename, is proven on scratch after `up`, in the with-data proof, once its rows are written. Each call runs in its own transaction that's rolled back, with a 30-second statement timeout. A failure stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the function and the error, so a broken one never ships, and the developer fixes the definition in the same migration. A function or procedure callable with no arguments gets `SELECT * FROM f()` or `CALL p()` automatically. If it declares `proof` lines, those run instead, each in its own rolled-back transaction, in the order written, and any failure stops `makemigrations`, naming that `proof`. One that needs arguments and has no `proof` stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, asking for one. Nothing is skipped silently. A passing call can't show that a body still means what it did, such as a `s::text = 'old'` comparison, so a hit stays a decision too. A trigger function can't be called directly, so it's proven by a write that fires it: for each managed trigger on it, morm runs an insert, an update of every column or a delete, as the trigger's events need, under `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)`, after `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE`, and the plan must list that trigger. A write that doesn't fire it, such as under a `WHEN`, stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, asking for a `proof`, and each `proof` is a write checked the same way. A trigger function with no managed trigger on it, one that only a `TRUNCATE` trigger fires, and an event trigger function need a `proof` too, run as written.

reqs.text: - **What a call may touch.** A rollback undoes what a call does in the database, including volatile functions' writes, session settings and `NOTIFY`, and scratch is thrown away, so a moved sequence or an advisory lock doesn't matter. It can't undo what leaves the server, so morm's own calls and writes run as `_morm_proof`, a role morm creates on scratch if it's missing, which isn't superuser, has rights on every table, sequence and schema in that database, and has no `EXECUTE` on any function from an extension or in a language other than `sql` or `plpgsql`. The scratch user keeps those, and any it can't take from `_morm_proof` stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`. So a body that reaches `dblink`, an HTTP extension or `COPY ... PROGRAM` fails with `42501`, directly, through another function or through `EXECUTE`, and `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2`, asking for a `proof`. A `SECURITY DEFINER` function, or one in another language, gets past that role, so it always needs a `proof`. Each `proof` is one statement, and it runs with the scratch user's rights, because the developer wrote it and vouches for it: it must not reach outside Postgres, and morm can't check that. One that ends the transaction fails the same way as a failed call. A procedure that commits can't run in a transaction, so on `2D000` morm runs the same call with no transaction on a throwaway copy of that database, made with `CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE` and dropped afterwards.

A migration can stop and ask you to add a `proof` line to a managed function or procedure before it goes through, because a change under a function can break it in ways Postgres only shows when it's called, and morm won't ship one it can't call. morm really runs that call, on a scratch database, in a transaction it rolls back, with a 30-second timeout, so the call has to be safe to run, and it must not reach outside Postgres. PROGRAM` stops and asks for a `proof`. With a `proof`, morm runs what you wrote with your scratch user's rights and can't check it, so write a call that takes no outside action. Unmanaged functions can't be proven, because scratch can't see them, so they become a migration decision that names each one and says it may fail until it's rewritten. morm can only see them on the live database, so `migrate`, `rollback` or `rehearse` stops with exit code `3` and prints an ID, and you answer with `--decide ID=OPT` on that same command. morm keeps the answer in `_morm.decisions` on that database, and it covers only that migration, that version of it, that direction and that ID. So an answer on `migrate` doesn't cover `rollback`, an answer on `rehearse` doesn't reach production, and editing the migration or changing the function asks again.

reqs.text: **Same meaning when the text differs.** Postgres keeps an alias once it has one, so after cutover a `USING` view reads `FROM (t t JOIN t2 USING (n))` where the models' reads `FROM (t JOIN t2 USING (n))`, and a later rename of another column on that table prints the whole column list again. The view is the same, so neither is a change. Where the text of a view or `BEGIN ATOMIC` function differs from the model's, morm checks the meaning on the database that holds it. It builds the model's definition there under a temporary name, `WITH NO DATA` for a materialized view, reads both stored query trees, `pg_rewrite.ev_action` or `pg_proc.prosqlbody`, removes every `location`, `stmt_location`, `stmt_len`, `isNatural`, `alias` and `eref` field, compares what's left, and drops the temporary object. Both trees are on one database, so tables, columns and types compare by number, and the join's `usingClause` and every output name stay in. Equal is a match. Anything else is a difference, and so is a model definition that can't be built there. In the scratch proof a difference fails the proof and writes no file. Step 30's diff runs this check before it counts a text difference as a change, so `makemigrations` proposes nothing for a matching view. A match found while a migration is made stores the two texts, the database's and the model's, in `op_data`, and `migrate` copies that pair to the ledger. `verify` can't build anything on a live database, so it treats a live view as matching when its text and the model's are a pair the ledger holds, and any other text is drift. On a `pg_major` mismatch, step 34's replay runs the check in its temporary database in place of the pair.

reqs.text: **Column positions.** A `USING` view's text holds a column list, such as `t t(id, _morm_retired_0007_n, note, n)`, and Postgres applies it by position, so it's only right if the live table's columns sit where scratch's do. An unmanaged column on the live table moved them, and the view read that column and returned wrong rows with no error. morm finds a list with no parser: the object's stored query tree has an `alias` field with `colnames`. So `makemigrations` stores in `op_data` the columns of each table with a list, in order, and the columns each built object reads, from `pg_depend`. `migrate` preflight refuses with exit code `2`, naming the table and saying `--fast` handles it, when the live table's columns differ from the stored list, before the swap's first step. Each build's own transaction reads `pg_depend` for the new object, and if it reads any other column, the transaction rolls back and the migration stops as `failed`, because a column can change after preflight.

reqs.text: **A cutover gives way.** A cutover can deadlock with an app transaction: one that touched the table and then reads the view waits on the cutover, while the cutover waits on it. Once either has waited for `deadlock_timeout`, Postgres kills one of them. So by default a migration never kills a live app transaction. Each attempt runs with `lock_timeout` set to `[migrations] cutover_lock_timeout`, default `"50ms"`, well under `deadlock_timeout`, so the attempt rolls back before Postgres looks for a deadlock. An attempt that hits the timeout with `55P03`, or that Postgres picks as a deadlock's victim with `40P01`, changes nothing, and morm waits `cutover_pause`, default `"250ms"`, and tries again, up to `cutover_attempts`, default `600`, so a cutover that can't get in gives up after about 3 minutes. The three settings are plain values in `morm.toml`, and they hold for the cutover's inverse too. An attempt holds its first lock through every later wait, so `migrate` and `rollback` preflight read the server's `deadlock_timeout`, and each lock in that cutover waits `min(cutover_lock_timeout, deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks))`, where `locks` is the number of locks the cutover takes. So a whole attempt stays under half of `deadlock_timeout` however many locks it takes, with no setting to change, and when that wait is shorter than `cutover_lock_timeout`, the output says so, naming the three numbers and the wait. Postgres rounds `lock_timeout` to a whole millisecond and reads 0 as no timeout, so morm rounds the wait down to a whole millisecond, and when that's under 1 ms preflight refuses with exit code `2` before the swap's first step, naming the three numbers. The message says how to go on: raise `deadlock_timeout`, or `cutover_lock_timeout` when it's set under 1 ms, or write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` for a maintenance window. After the last attempt the cutover step stops as `failed` with exit code `2` and nothing changed, saying how many attempts it made and that `migrate --resume` carries on from there. The sync trigger stays, so the shadow column keeps up while the migration waits. `--resume` starts this step again with a full set of attempts, after dropping and rebuilding any materialized view built beside the old one, because a copy that sat waiting is no longer as late as possible. `rollback --failed` also still works. `--terminate-blockers`, on `migrate` and `rollback`, is the one way to push a cutover through. While an attempt runs, a second connection calls `pg_terminate_backend` every 10 ms on every backend `pg_blocking_pids` names for it, and each one goes in `_morm.history` with its user and application name. Those transactions die, and their apps lose the connection. It acts only during a cutover, never in any other step, and each lock waits `cutover_lock_timeout`, with no shorter wait and no `deadlock_timeout` check. A longer wait is no substitute, because Postgres may pick the cutover as the victim every time. A role that may not terminate a backend gets `42501`, and the step stops as `failed`, changing nothing. `pg_signal_backend` gives that right.

reqs.text: - **Every path is checked statically.** A real call proves only the path it takes, and Postgres checks a plpgsql statement only when it first runs, so a column dropped from a branch the call misses passes R-1066 with no error. So every managed plpgsql function and procedure R-1066 proves is also checked by `plpgsql_check`, at the same point in the with-data proof. It needs no preload and runs nothing. morm calls `plpgsql_check_function_tb` with the function's `regprocedure`, `fatal_errors => false` and `all_warnings => true`, so overloads stay apart and every finding comes back at once. A procedure, an event trigger function and a polymorphic function need nothing more. A trigger function fails with `22023` `missing trigger relation` with no table, so it's checked once for each managed trigger on it, with that trigger's table as the second argument, plus `oldtable` and `newtable` from `pg_trigger` when the trigger has transition tables, because without them a healthy function gets `42P01`. A trigger function with no managed trigger has no table to check against, so it must declare a `proof`, as a body using `EXECUTE` must, and without one `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2`, asking for one. That `proof` is all it gets. A `language sql` function fails with `22023` here, so morm never sends one, and R-1066 alone covers it. With no managed plpgsql function in scope, none of this runs, and the extension isn't needed.

reqs.text: - **Without the extension.** With a managed plpgsql function in scope, `makemigrations` writes nothing if the check can't run: `plpgsql_check` isn't in `pg_available_extensions` on scratch, there's no template and the scratch user can't make it, or the clone fails or holds no extension. It names each function and says what to do: install the extension on the scratch server, `postgresql-NN-plpgsql-check` from PGDG, with R-1077's statements printed in full when the scratch user isn't a superuser, or add `proof` lines to the function and accept the risk. Accepting is a decision that names the function and says only the paths its `proof` lines take are proven. A function with no `proof` can't be accepted, even one R-1066 would call by itself, so `makemigrations` stops with exit code `2` while any function in scope has none. Once each has a `proof` the decision is open, its default refuses, and `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` until it's accepted. Accepted functions still get their real calls.

reqs.text: - **Findings stop `makemigrations`.** Any finding at level `error` is an open decision, so it stops `makemigrations` with exit code `3`, naming the function, the line and the message, with no file written. No other level stops it, apart from R-1080. A healthy function can get a false `error`, from a temp table, a table created in the body or by the caller, a record filled by `EXECUTE`, a record with different fields by branch, `set_config` of `search_path`, or a constant `1/0`. There are two ways past a false one. reqs.text: - **A narrowing is a decision.** An `int` variable reading a column now `bigint` isn't an error. It works until a value needs the new type, and with default arguments the check reports nothing. With `all_warnings` it's a finding at level `performance`, with SQLSTATE `42804` and detail `cast "bigint" value to "integer" type`. A widening looks the same, so morm reads both type names from the detail, and it's a narrowing when `pg_cast` holds that pair with a `castcontext` other than `i`. Each narrowing is a decision that names the function, the line and both types, and says the function fails once a value doesn't fit. Its default refuses, so `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` until it's accepted. Every other `all_warnings` finding is ignored. A length or precision limit doesn't show up: `varchar(3)` reading `text` is a cast `pg_cast` calls implicit, and `numeric(6,2)` reading `numeric(20,4)` gave no finding at all, so R-1092 works from the column's definitions instead.

It caught a dropped column in a constant string and in a `format` of constants, and reported nothing for `EXECUTE 'SELECT ' || c || ' FROM t'`. reqs.text: - **morm won't run a disabled check.** With `plpgsql_check.mode` set to `disabled`, the check returns no findings and only a `NOTICE`, so it looks like a pass. Before checking, in the session that runs the check, morm reads `current_setting('plpgsql_check.mode', true)`, which shows a role or connection setting even before the library loads, and is NULL when nothing sets it. It also reads each function's `pg_proc.proconfig`, because `SET plpgsql_check.mode = 'disabled'` on a function turns the check off for that function alone, and `current_setting` doesn't show it. Either one stops `makemigrations` with exit code `2`, naming the setting and any function.

**The extension in CI.** Every job whose tests run `makemigrations` over a managed plpgsql function installs the extension into its running service, which needs no restart. These are `integration` and `pooler` in `ci.yml`, `property` and `full-chain` in `nightly.yml`, `test` in `release.yml`, and T-0172's job:

```yaml
- name: Install plpgsql_check
  env:
    PG_CONTAINER: ${{ job.services.postgres.id }}
  run: |
    docker exec "$PG_CONTAINER" apt-get update
    docker exec "$PG_CONTAINER" apt-get install -y "postgresql-$MORM_TEST_PG_MAJOR-plpgsql-check"
```

A new `ci.yml` job, `no-plpgsql-check`, runs the plain `postgres` image on Postgres 15–18 with no install step, because R-1078 needs a server without the extension. Its test has its own Cargo feature, `no_plpgsql_check`, with `required-features`, as `pooler` does. The feature sits on `morm-tests`, because `integration` runs `morm-migrate` with `--all-features`. The `ci` job waits for the new job, and `tests/tests/repo_policy.rs` gets its command, with `docker exec ` added to `SETUP`.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the managed function rows:

> **Silencing a check can hide a real break.** When a migration changes something a managed plpgsql function names, morm runs `plpgsql_check` on that function, and any `error` stops the migration. There are two ways past an error, and neither one fixes anything. If the finding was real, the function ships broken and fails in production the first time that line runs.
>
> **What each one does.** A `PERFORM 'PRAGMA:...'` line goes in the function. It changes what `plpgsql_check` looks at, on this migration and every later one, and when the function runs it's only a string, so it does nothing. A decision leaves the function alone and lets that one finding through on that one migration. It's recorded in the migration's `meta.json`, and the next migration that reaches the function checks it again.
>
> ```sql
> -- Tell the checker what it can't see. It still checks every other line.
> PERFORM 'PRAGMA:TABLE: report_rows (id bigint, total numeric)';
> PERFORM 'PRAGMA:TYPE: r (id bigint, total numeric)';
>
> -- Stop checking until this block ends. Keep the block as small as you can.
> BEGIN
>   PERFORM 'PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK';
>   PERFORM 1 / 0;
> END;
> ```
>
> ```
> makemigrations --decide ID=OPT     # morm prints the ID and the options
> ```
>
> **When it's right.** Only when you've read the finding and can say why it's false, such as a temp table the function creates, or a record it fills with `EXECUTE`. Prefer `PRAGMA:TABLE` and `PRAGMA:TYPE`, because the checker keeps reading every other line. Use `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` only when those can't describe the problem. Use a decision when you won't change the function.
>
> **What you give up.** No line under `PRAGMA:DISABLE:CHECK` is checked, on this migration or any later one, so a column dropped from one of them passes. The checker believes a `TABLE` or `TYPE` line over the database, so one that no longer matches hides a break too. An accepted finding stays unfixed, and morm won't stop that migration for it again. After that, only a `proof` that runs that line can catch a real break, and a call proves only the path it takes.

reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside that notice. A call proves only the path it takes, so a passing `proof` says nothing about a branch it didn't reach, and a function can have several `proof` lines to cover the paths that matter. `plpgsql_check` reads every branch without running it, but it can only read what's in the source. A query built at run time with `EXECUTE` isn't checked, so a function using `EXECUTE` must have a `proof`. morm finds it with a word search, so the word in a comment or a string asks for a `proof` too. That `proof` proves only the query its one call builds, and any other query the body can build stays unproven until production runs it. A trigger function with no trigger on it has no table to check against, so it must have a `proof`, and that `proof` is all it gets, so any path it doesn't take stays unproven until production runs it. `plpgsql_check` can't see a length or precision limit, so `varchar(3)` reading a longer `text` column, or `numeric(6,2)` reading a wider `numeric`, gets no finding. So after any change to a column's type, length or precision, even a widening, morm walks everything that reaches that column, of any kind, and repeats until nothing new turns up. It follows `pg_depend` to every object that depends on what it has found, and it searches function source for the name of everything it has found, including operator and aggregate symbols. Everything it finds goes on one list, as one decision per migration. A function using `EXECUTE` starts the walk too, even one that doesn't name the column, because no tool can see what a built query reads, and whatever calls it is found by name. Being on the list doesn't mean something is broken. The search reads text, so a common name can bring in something that has nothing to do with the change. The list holds only what carries code or an expression: functions, procedures, views, triggers, policies, rules, expression and partial indexes, and non-constant defaults and checks. Any such object on the changed table is listed, even one on another column, because a whole row such as `to_jsonb(x)` carries the changed column without naming it. A default or a check on another column that only calls built-ins, such as `DEFAULT now()`, isn't listed, because it can't depend on the changed column. A built-in that runs query text it's given, such as `query_to_xml`, `ts_stat` or `ts_rewrite` with a query, or reads every table in a schema or the database, such as `schema_to_xml` or `database_to_xml`, or a table or a cursor it's given by name at run time, such as `table_to_xml` or `cursor_to_xml`, counts as code, so a default or a check that calls one is listed, on any column. A plain index, a `NOT NULL` or a constant default isn't listed, because it can't hold a stale type. morm walks only what it can see. On scratch that's your managed objects, so `makemigrations` lists those. Scratch can't see an unmanaged object, so that part of the walk only works in the preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse`, on the live database, and that's where the first warning about one comes, as a list of its own. The walk follows objects, not values, and that's its stated limit. So every widening's decision carries this line, and a widening with nothing to list still prints it in `makemigrations` output and as a comment in the migration, without stopping: `Values can now exceed the old limit anywhere that reads them, including code morm can't see.` `pass_f(max(n))` shows why. A function that only receives the column's value as an argument, and names nothing, isn't found, though what calls it is, because a value can flow through arguments, other tables, application code and other services, further than any tool can follow. So read what a listed object calls, and treat everything that reads that column as able to see a value the old limit kept out. A query built from data in a table leaves nothing in the catalog or in any source to find, so that shows up when production runs it. Your Rust code is on that side of the line too, because the walk reads nothing but the database. The compiler checks a model field only against the SQL type declared for it: `i64` on `integer` is a compile error, and `i32` on `bigint` compiles. That pair gets a range CHECK, so the column can't store a value the field can't read, and if one still arrives, because the CHECK was removed outside morm, decoding returns `OutOfRange`, never a wrapped value. `db.check_schema()` runs at startup and refuses a column of a kind the field can't decode, such as `text` for an integer field, which is a question of compatibility, so it doesn't show that a field or the code using it is ready for a wider value. A decision proves nothing. It says what's listed may break and leaves the reading to you, and it can't show you where a limit sits or which queries a built string can become. Read each object and what it calls before you accept it, and after that only production shows whether a value fits. If you accept a decision because `plpgsql_check` isn't installed, your `proof` lines are all that's proven. Neither check shows that a body still means what it did, such as a `s::text = 'old'` comparison that stops matching.

reqs.text: **A decision about a database object keeps its ID across a rerun.** A decision about a database object, of any kind, gets an ID built from the migration's `id`, the decision's kind and the object's signature, plus a hash of its source, in the form `<id>/<kind>/<signature>/<hash>`. So the ID stays the same across a rerun, and changes if the object's source does. `makemigrations` and the preflight of `migrate`, `rollback` and `rehearse` build it with the same code, because an unmanaged function already accepted on scratch must match on the live database and not be asked about again. The hash is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the source. Every read below runs with `search_path` set to `pg_catalog`, because otherwise the text depends on the session: the same function reads `sf(ty,integer)` in one and `app.sf(app.ty,integer)` in another, and a view, a default and a check read the same way. A function's signature is its `regprocedure` text, and its source is `prosrc`, or `pg_get_function_sqlbody(oid)` when `prosqlbody` isn't null, because a `BEGIN ATOMIC` or `RETURN` body leaves `prosrc` empty, and hashing that would miss an edit. A view's signature is its `regclass` text, and its source is `pg_get_viewdef`. A default's signature is its table's `regclass` text and the column's name, and its source is `pg_get_expr`. A check's signature is the `regclass` text of its table, or the `regtype` text of its domain, and the constraint's name, and its source is `pg_get_constraintdef`. Any other kind's signature is the `identity` column of `pg_identify_object`, and its source is what `pg_get_triggerdef`, `pg_get_indexdef`, `pg_get_ruledef`, `pg_get_constraintdef`, `pg_get_statisticsobjdef`, `pg_get_partkeydef` or `pg_get_expr` prints for it, where one of those fits, and otherwise its signature alone. A decision that lists several objects has the signature `list`, and its hash covers the sorted lines `<signature> <hash>`, one per object, so adding or changing any of them gives a new ID. `meta.json` keeps those lines with an accepted list, so a later preflight can leave out what's already accepted. A `BEGIN ATOMIC` body is deparsed, and so are a view, a default and a check, so a rename in an earlier step of the same migration changes the source, and with it the hash and the ID, of the object or the list holding it. `--resume` then asks again, because the recorded answer is for the old ID. That's safe: it costs one extra stop. A migration's `id` doesn't depend on any answer, so the ID a stopped run prints still holds when the same command runs again with the answer. A name can hold a space or an `=`, so morm prints each ID quoted for the shell, and `--decide` splits at the last `=`. `meta.json` records each answer with the direction of the decision it answers, `up` or `down`, and a decision open in both directions is recorded for both.

reqs.text: - **Answering a decision at `migrate`.** Some decisions only appear against the live database, in preflight, because scratch can't see what they're about. `migrate` takes `--decide ID=OPT` for them, in the same form as `makemigrations`, once per answer. It never prompts for a decision, `--yes` answers none, and each open one is printed with its ID, evidence and options, in `--json` too, before the run stops with exit code `3`. An answer stands only for the same migration id, checksum, direction and decision ID, so an `up` answer doesn't cover `rollback`, and editing the migration cancels it. A decision is open unless `meta.json` holds an answer to it for this direction, or `_morm.decisions` holds a row matching all four. An answer is committed to `_morm.decisions`, with its history row, as soon as its decision opens, while the run holds the advisory lock. So it survives a failed or killed run, a rerun or step 34's `migrate --resume` doesn't need it again unless the decision's ID has changed, as step 32 says of a deparsed body, and a run that stops on a second decision keeps the first answer. A new answer to the same decision replaces the row and gets its own history row. An answer that refuses stops the run with exit code `2`, because the decision is answered and the guard holds. Preflight runs before each migration, so an answer to a later migration in the run waits for it. An ID no migration in the run opened is reported and recorded nowhere, and an option the decision doesn't offer stops the run with exit code `1`, with nothing recorded. `--plan` shows what's open and records nothing.

reqs.text: - **Answering a decision at `rollback`.** `rollback` runs step 33's preflight, with each op's own checks, before each migration it undoes, in direction `down`, in every form: `--last`, `--to`, `--orphans` and `--failed`. It reads `meta.json` from the ledger, so the search and the checks work when the files are gone. A decision it opens stops it with exit code `3`, and `rollback --decide ID=OPT` answers it, under step 33's rules for `--decide`, recorded in `_morm.decisions` with direction `down` and a history row. An answer given to `migrate` survives `migrate --resume`, and one given to `rollback` survives a rerun of a `rollback` that was killed.

A decision it opens stops it with exit code `3`, printing the ID, evidence and options, and `rehearse --decide ID=OPT` answers it, once per answer, in the same form as `migrate` and `rollback` and under step 33's rules for `--decide`, recorded in that database's `_morm.decisions` with the pass's direction and a history row. An ID open in more than one pass is answered for each pass of that run that opens it, with a row for each direction. A stop leaves the database where it stopped, so a stop in the `down` pass has its `up` pass already applied. So `rehearse` records each pass and migration it finishes in `_morm.history`, and a rerun on that database carries on from where it stopped, runs nothing twice, and can't report a pass because nothing is pending. Answers stay on the database they were given on. They don't answer `migrate` anywhere else, so production is asked for its own, and a restored backup holds none given after it was taken, so `rehearse` asks for those there. A production database still exits with code `2` first, with nothing recorded.

reqs.text: - **What the walk lists.** R-1038's walk can find anything, and it keeps only what carries code or an expression, because nothing else can hold a stale type. That holds for every decision the walk opens, after any op. morm decides it from the catalog, with no SQL parser. An object is kept if it's one of these: a `pg_proc` row of any `prokind`; a view or a materialized view, a `pg_class` row with `relkind` `v` or `m`; a `pg_rewrite` row; a `pg_trigger` row with `tgisinternal` false; a `pg_policy` row; an index whose `pg_index` row has `indexprs` or `indpred`; a `pg_attrdef` row, or a `pg_constraint` row with `conbin`, whose stored expression isn't constant; a `pg_constraint` row whose `conindid` index has `indexprs` or `indpred`, such as an exclusion constraint over an expression; a `pg_statistic_ext` row with `stxexprs`; a partitioned table whose `pg_partitioned_table` row has `partexprs`; a `pg_publication_rel` row with `prqual`; or a row of any catalog this rule doesn't name, so a kind it never names costs one line and is never hidden. An expression is constant when the text of its `adbin` or `conbin` holds no node but `CONST`, `RELABELTYPE` and `FUNCEXPR`, when every `FUNCEXPR` is a cast, with `funcformat` `1` or `2`, and when every `funcid` is below `16384`, so a cast a user wrote counts as code. So `0` on a `numeric(6,2)` column, `'ab'` on a `varchar(3)`, `1.5::numeric(6,2)` and `'{}'` are constant, and `now()`, `nextval(...)`, `1 + 1`, `ARRAY[1, 2]` and a default through a domain aren't. A check that reads a column holds a `VAR` node, so it's never constant, and `CHECK (true)` is. Anything that isn't sure comes out as not constant, which costs one line. On a table with a column whose type, length or precision changes, a default or a check on its other columns that only calls built-ins isn't kept either, because it can't depend on the changed column. That's a `pg_attrdef` row that isn't a generated column's expression, or a `pg_constraint` row with `conbin`, whose `pg_depend` rows against that table all name its other columns, with none against the changed column or the table as a whole, and whose other `pg_depend` rows are each against a sequence or an object with an OID below `16384`, and which calls no built-in that runs query text or reads whole tables. Those built-ins count as code, because what they run can read any column: the `query_to_xml` family, which is `query_to_xml`, `query_to_xmlschema` and `query_to_xml_and_xmlschema`; `schema_to_xml`, `schema_to_xmlschema`, `schema_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, `database_to_xml`, `database_to_xmlschema` and `database_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read every table in a schema or the database, so their output holds the changed column's values and the xmlschema forms its type; `table_to_xml`, `table_to_xmlschema` and `table_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read the table they're given as a `regclass` that can be built at run time, such as `('t'::text)::regclass`, so no `pg_depend` row names that table; `cursor_to_xml` and `cursor_to_xmlschema`, which read whatever query a cursor opened elsewhere runs, found only by its name; `ts_stat`; and `ts_rewrite(tsquery, text)`. morm finds such a call in the stored expression, as a `FUNCEXPR` in the text of its `adbin` or `conbin` whose `funcid` is one of them, looked up in `pg_catalog` by name and argument types, so it doesn't rest on `pg_depend`. So `DEFAULT now()`, `DEFAULT nextval(...)`, `DEFAULT ARRAY[1, 2]` and `CHECK (a > abs(-1))` on another column aren't kept, while a default or a check there that calls a user's function, or goes through a domain or a user's cast, is, because it holds a `pg_depend` row against that object, and so is one that calls one of those built-ins, such as `CHECK (b > 0 AND query_to_xml('SELECT max(n)::numeric(6,2) FROM t', true, false, '') IS NOT NULL)` on another column `b`. A check holding a whole row, such as `to_jsonb(t)`, has its `pg_depend` row against the table as a whole, and so does a check that reads no column, so both stay on, and so does a generated column. On the changed column itself the rule above stands, so a default there that isn't constant is kept. Not kept, and walked all the same where a row leads to them, because they're how the walk reaches what lies beyond: a table and its columns, a partition, a TOAST table, a type of any kind, such as a row type, an array, a domain or a composite type, a sequence, a plain index, a plain statistics object, a constant default, a `pg_constraint` row with no expression, which is a `NOT NULL`, a primary key, a unique constraint or a foreign key, an operator, a cast and an operator class. A `NOT NULL` has `conbin` null on Postgres 18, where it's a `pg_constraint` row, and it has no row on a table before that, so both come out the same. A function in `pg_catalog` or `information_schema` is never found, by a row, by the source search or through a trigger, because it ships with Postgres, so the `RI_FKey_*` functions behind a foreign key aren't kept, and a word that names one doesn't lead on to everything that calls it. An object Postgres keeps as an internal part of another, with `deptype` `i`, is walked, and it's left off the list only when the object it's part of is on it. So a view's stored query and an exclusion constraint's index are left off, and a generated column's expression stays on, because its column isn't listed. The list test is the one place the walk's code looks at a kind, apart from a trigger's function.

Those built-ins count as code, because what they run can read any column: the `query_to_xml` family, which is `query_to_xml`, `query_to_xmlschema` and `query_to_xml_and_xmlschema`; `schema_to_xml`, `schema_to_xmlschema`, `schema_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, `database_to_xml`, `database_to_xmlschema` and `database_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read every table in a schema or the database, so their output holds the changed column's values and the xmlschema forms its type; `table_to_xml`, `table_to_xmlschema` and `table_to_xml_and_xmlschema`, which read the table they're given as a `regclass` that can be built at run time, such as `('t'::text)::regclass`, so no `pg_depend` row names that table; `cursor_to_xml` and `cursor_to_xmlschema`, which read whatever query a cursor opened elsewhere runs, found only by its name; `ts_stat`; and `ts_rewrite(tsquery, text)`. morm finds such a call in the stored expression, as a `FUNCEXPR` in the text of its `adbin` or `conbin` whose `funcid` is one of them, looked up in `pg_catalog` by name and argument types, so it doesn't rest on `pg_depend`. A check holding a whole row, such as `to_jsonb(t)`, has its `pg_depend` row against the table as a whole, and so does a check that reads no column, so both stay on, and so does a generated column. On the changed column itself the rule above stands, so a default there that isn't constant is kept. Not kept, and walked all the same where a row leads to them, because they're how the walk reaches what lies beyond: a table and its columns, a partition, a TOAST table, a type of any kind, such as a row type, an array, a domain or a composite type, a sequence, a plain index, a plain statistics object, a constant default, a `pg_constraint` row with no expression, which is a `NOT NULL`, a primary key, a unique constraint or a foreign key, an operator, a cast and an operator class. A `NOT NULL` has `conbin` null on Postgres 18, where it's a `pg_constraint` row, and it has no row on a table before that, so both come out the same. A function in `pg_catalog` or `information_schema` is never found, by a row, by the source search or through a trigger, because it ships with Postgres, so the `RI_FKey_*` functions behind a foreign key aren't kept, and a word that names one doesn't lead on to everything that calls it. An object Postgres keeps as an internal part of another, with `deptype` `i`, is walked, and it's left off the list only when the object it's part of is on it. So a view's stored query and an exclusion constraint's index are left off, and a generated column's expression stays on, because its column isn't listed. The list test is the one place the walk's code looks at a kind, apart from a trigger's function.

reqs.text: - **Reading a column whose type changed.** A migration can change a column's type under a running binary, so each field also decodes every column type in its family, through the decoder for the column's real type, which step 14 chooses once per statement. These are the families, and there are no others: a field of a Rust integer type reads `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint` and `numeric(p,0)` with any `p`, and never a `numeric` with a scale or with no precision; `Decimal` reads `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in its 28 digits; `morm::Numeric` reads `numeric` with any precision and scale, or with none, and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, as `Decimal` does; `String` reads `text`, and `varchar` with any length or none; a `String` built against `char(n)` reads `char` with any length, through a decoder that trims trailing spaces back to `n`, because Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and treats them as insignificant, so on `char(4)` `'ab  '` reads as `'ab '`, as it did on `char(3)`, and a value with no spaces to trim, such as `'abcd'`, reads whole; `DateTime<Utc>` and `Timestamp` read `timestamptz` with any precision, and `NaiveDateTime` reads `timestamp` with any precision; and an array reads an array of its element's family. A write goes as the column type the field was built against, and Postgres converts it to the column's real type, so a value the column can't hold, such as a number with more digits before the point than it allows or a text longer than its length, gets the database's error for that write. reqs.text: - **Decoding follows the column's real type.** When a statement is prepared, morm reads each result column's type from the row description Postgres returns, chooses each field's decoder from it once, and keeps that choice with the statement in its cache entry. A `query_typed` call, which has no cache entry, chooses once from its own result's row description. The internal query entry point then reads all of that statement's rows through `from_row` when every column has the type the binary was built against, so that path is unchanged, and through `from_row_as` with the statement's choice otherwise, deciding once before the first row and never per row. A re-prepare after a migration, on `0A000` as R-0718 says, chooses again, so a statement cached before a cutover picks the new column type's decoder. Every statement is prepared with each parameter's type from `Param`, as `query_typed` sends it, so a parameter goes as the column type the binary was built against and Postgres converts it when it's written: a widened column takes every value the binary writes, and a value a narrowed one can't hold gets the database's error for that write.
