reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside the `Decimal` and `Numeric` rows. `Decimal` holds up to 28 significant digits. The limit comes from `rust_decimal`, which keeps every value in a fixed 16 bytes, as a 96-bit whole number and a scale, so it needs no heap and is `Copy`. A `Decimal` on a `numeric(p,s)` with `p` or `s` above 28 is a compile error. A `numeric` with no precision compiles with `Decimal`, because existing tables have it, and a value that doesn't fit fails at read with `Error::Decimal`. So does a value past 28 digits in a column a migration has widened. A `Decimal` field also reads `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, because every one of their values fits in 28 digits, so a column changed from `numeric` to an integer type doesn't stop a running app built for `numeric`. When that change drops a scale, Postgres would round what such an app writes, so `migrate` holds it for `contract`, and an app built for that scale that starts after it fails the schema check morm runs when a pool starts, rather than rounding what it writes. `morm::Numeric` reads `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` the same way. morm never rounds a `Decimal`, on read or on write. Use `morm::Numeric` when values can exceed 28 digits, or be `NaN` or `Infinity`, or when you don't know a column's range.

reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside the rolling deploy rows. A type change never stops a running app. An app built before a migration changes a column's type, length or precision keeps working through it, and still starts after it, apart from the one case below, while the column stays in the same family: integers; `numeric`, where `Decimal` and `Numeric` fields also read `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`; `text` and `varchar`; `char`; or timestamps. `timestamp` and `timestamptz` stay apart, because a change between them shifts every value by the time zone of the session that runs it, with no error. It reads each value through the decoder for the column's real type, chosen once per statement, so it costs nothing when the types match. After a widening, every value the old column could hold reads as before, and a value only the new column can hold fails on its own: an integer field returns `Error::OutOfRange` naming the column, and `Decimal` returns `Error::Decimal` past its 28 digits. `Numeric` and `String` read every value whole, apart from `char`: Postgres pads a `char` value with spaces to its length and treats them as insignificant, so a field built for `char(3)` reads `char(4)`'s `'ab  '` as `'ab '`, as it did before, and `'abcd'` whole. After a narrowing, every value fits the old field, so every read works, and a write the column can no longer hold, such as a number with too many digits before the point or a text too long, gets the database's error for that write. Some narrowings would change a write with no error instead: a lower scale stores `1.0051` as `1.01`, and `numeric(12,2)` to `integer` stores `1.25` as `1`, a lower timestamp precision stores `.123456` as `.123`, and a shorter `varchar` or `char` stores `'abc  '` as `'abc'`. morm never runs one of those while an app built for the old shape may be running, and in an ordinary online `migrate` it always assumes one is, without trying to find out. So `migrate` refuses it, naming the column, what would change, and the two ways to run it: `migrate --phase contract` once the new release is out everywhere, or `makemigrations --fast` for a maintenance window with apps stopped. An old app never sees one: through the rollout its column keeps the old shape, and every value it writes is stored as written. So an old app keeps running through the deploy, because the narrowing waits until it's gone. Only a build brought back after `contract` has run, such as a rollback of the app to an older release, would write to the narrower column, so it's refused at startup: morm runs `check_schema` when each pool starts, and `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming the column and what would change, so the app fails loudly rather than storing values other than the ones it writes, unless that pool is set to `check_schema = "off"`. A narrowing that raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit still lets such a build start. `rollback` holds the same narrowings when one is the down of a widening, and runs it with `--phase contract` once every app runs the release built for the narrower shape, or `--fast` with apps stopped. Such a narrowing also changes the rows already stored, so a `1.0051` already in the column becomes `1.01`, and `makemigrations` asks you to accept that as a `lossy` decision before it writes the migration. `migrate` and `rollback` count the rows in the live table it would change, and when there are any they stop and ask, showing the count, answered with `--decide`. When there are none they run with no question, so rolling back a widening asks only when rows were written since that need the wider column. Nothing read is ever rounded. A change to an unrelated kind, such as `text` to `integer`, still fails the startup check.

reqs.text: **A narrowing Postgres would change silently waits for `contract`.** Postgres rounds or cuts some writes to a narrower column with no error, so an app built for the old shape would store a value other than the one it wrote, and nothing would tell it. These are the silent narrowings, and there are no others: a lower scale, where a `numeric` with no precision counts as unlimited and `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` count as 0, so `1.0051` written to a column changed from `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)` is stored as `1.01`, `1.00005` from `numeric` to `numeric(20,4)` as `1.0001`, and `1.25` from `numeric(12,2)` to `integer` as `1`; a lower precision on `timestamptz` or `timestamp`, where no precision counts as 6, so `.123456` from `timestamptz` to `timestamptz(3)` is stored as `.123`; and a shorter length on `varchar` or `char`, where `text` and a `varchar` with no length count as unlimited, because Postgres cuts trailing spaces to fit, so `'abc  '` from `text` to `varchar(3)` is stored as `'abc'`, and `'abc '` from `char(4)` to `char(3)` as `'abc'`. The same change to an array's element type is one too, because Postgres applies it to each element, so `{1.0051}` from `numeric(20,4)[]` to `numeric(20,2)[]` is stored as `{1.01}`. morm reads which it is from the column's old and new definition, as `format_type` prints them, with no SQL parser. A change that's one of these and widens something else, such as `numeric(8,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, is one. Every other narrowing raises a real error on a write that doesn't fit, such as fewer digits before the point, `bigint` to `integer`, `numeric(12,0)` to `integer`, or a shorter length for a value whose extra characters aren't all spaces, so it runs online as R-0612 says, with no gate. In online mode, which is a live run of a migration `makemigrations` wrote without `--fast`, morm always assumes an app built for the old shape is still running, and never tries to detect one. So `makemigrations` puts every step of a silent narrowing in `contract`, the online swap's shadow column, sync trigger and copy included, because the sync trigger would already narrow what an old app writes. The same holds for a migration `revert` writes, because a widening's down is a narrowing. It runs only under `migrate --phase contract`, which the operator runs once the new release is out everywhere. `makemigrations --fast` writes it in the one-transaction form, because `--fast` means a maintenance window with apps stopped. That form takes phase `contract` too, and plain `migrate` runs it. Plain `migrate` refuses the online form in preflight with exit code `2`, before that migration's first step, naming the table and column, the old and new definition, the silent change it would cause, such as `1.0051` stored as `1.01`, and the two ways to run it: `migrate --phase contract` once the new release is out everywhere, or `makemigrations --fast` for a maintenance window with apps stopped. `--phase expand` runs the migration's other `expand` steps and leaves the narrowing pending for `contract`.

reqs.text: **Counting the rows a silent narrowing would change.** Before `rollback` undoes, or `migrate` runs, a step that's one of R-1108's silent narrowings, its preflight counts the live rows that step would change, on the live database. morm builds the count from the column's old and new definition as `format_type` prints them, with no SQL parser. A row counts when the change would leave it a value that isn't equal, in the old type, to the one it holds, and the change raises no error on it. For a lower scale `s`, where `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` count as 0, that's `col <> round(col, s)`. For a lower timestamp precision `p`, it's `col <> CAST(col AS timestamptz(p))`, or `timestamp(p)`. For a shorter length `n`, to `varchar(n)`, it's `length(col) > n AND length(rtrim(col, ' ')) <= n`, and to `char(n)` from `text` or `varchar`, it's `col <> rtrim(col, ' ') AND length(rtrim(col, ' ')) <= n`, because a `char` value loses its trailing spaces when read as text. From `char` to a shorter `char`, no row counts, because Postgres treats a `char` value's trailing spaces as insignificant, so `'abc '` in `char(4)` and `'abc'` in `char(3)` are equal. On an array, a row counts when any element does, through `unnest`. A `NULL` never counts, and neither does a row the change refuses with an error, such as `'abcd'` into `varchar(3)` or `NaN` into `integer`, because that row stops the change instead. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, each of these counts matched the rows `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` changed, compared in the old type, including `-1.0050` to `numeric(20,2)`, `1.50` and `-1.50` to `integer`, `9999.9999` from `numeric(8,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, `'ab '` from `text` to `char(3)`, and `{{1.0051},{2}}`. The count is one `SELECT count(*)` per column, in a read-only transaction of its own, with `statement_timeout` off, so a role's timeout can't leave it unknown. It takes only `ACCESS SHARE`, so reads and writes go on while it runs: on both versions, an `UPDATE`, an `INSERT` and a `DELETE` from another session with a `500ms` `lock_timeout` went through while it was held. No index can answer it, so it reads the whole table, and Postgres can run it as a parallel sequential scan. It always runs to the end, however big the table, because only a full read shows that no row would change. That stays cheap beside the change itself, because every silent narrowing rewrites the whole table and its indexes, under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` in the one-transaction form, or copies every row in the online form: on both versions, the table's file changed for `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)`, `timestamptz` to `timestamptz(3)`, `varchar(10)` and `text` to `varchar(3)`, and `numeric(20,4)[]` to `numeric(20,2)[]`, and stayed the same for a widening. So the count adds one read of what the change reads and rewrites anyway. On a table of 10 million rows and 1.2 GB, held in memory, with two parallel workers, it took 0.31 s on both versions, while the change took 15.4 s on 18.6 and 16.6 s on 17.11. A huge table takes as long as one sequential read of it, and like any long read the count holds back vacuum for that time. Where R-1108 or R-1110 holds the step, it counts only once the hold lets the step through, so a refused run stops at once without reading the table. The count is taken as of preflight. The rows it's about are the ones apps built for the wider shape wrote, and those holds mean such apps no longer write when it runs: `--phase contract` runs once every app runs the release built for the narrower shape, and `--fast` with apps stopped. It's a preflight check of the op, so `rehearse` runs it in each pass, as step 40 says, and a rehearsal on real data shows the count before production does.

reqs.text: **`check_schema` runs when a pool starts.** morm runs `check_schema` by itself on every pool, before the pool serves anything, so a build that doesn't match the schema refuses to start. `Db::connect`, `connect_as` and `connect_to` run it on the first connection their pool opens, before they return, and return `Error::SchemaMismatch` when it fails, holding every finding. Each finding names the table and column, the definition the field was built against, the column's, and what's wrong: a missing column, an unrelated kind, one of R-1108's silent changes, such as `1.25` stored as `1.3`, one of R-0612's two insert cases, R-1190's partition column that its model's inserts send, or R-1194's `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column that its model's inserts send. So `let db = morm::Db::connect().await?;` stops the app at startup with that error, and none of the app's queries has run. A pool that `db.pool(name)` adds runs it before its first query. While it fails, every call through that pool returns the same error and runs the check again, so a replica that hadn't yet replayed a migration passes once it has. A pool that passed never checks again. Every pool runs it, `read_only` ones included, because a named pool can reach another host or log in as another role, and the pool must be able to serve every model the binary holds. The check covers every model in the binary, through the per-model column list, in one statement over the catalog, run through `query_typed` with no prepare round trip and no session state. So it works unchanged behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, where it checks the database PgBouncer connects that connection to, as the app's queries reach it. It costs one round trip on a pool's first connection and none after: checkouts, later connections and queries send nothing more. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with 2,000 tables in the catalog, reading every column of 200 tables of 20 columns, with type, `NOT NULL`, default and enum labels, took 3.2 to 3.7 ms on a local connection and returned about 95 KB, and 20 tables took 0.6 to 1.2 ms. The connection `morm-mgr` opens to run a data hook doesn't run it, because a hook runs in the middle of a migration, against a schema no build matches, and it uses raw SQL only. `db.check_schema()` runs the same check whenever it's called, whatever R-1117's setting says.

reqs.text: **Turning the startup check off.** The pool setting `check_schema` is `"on"` by default, and `"off"` turns R-1116's startup check off for that pool and nothing else. It's set like any pool setting: in `[pool]`, in one `[pools.<name>]`, or by `MORM_POOL_CHECK_SCHEMA` for the pool a process opens at startup. Any other value is `Error::Config`. With it off, that pool starts against any schema, so a missing column fails each query that names it, and a build brought back after `contract` stores rounded or cut values with no error.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **Turning off the startup check lets a build run against a schema it can't use.** morm runs `check_schema` when each pool starts, so a build that doesn't match the database refuses to start. `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming each table and column, the definition the build expects, the one the database has, and what's wrong, before any of your queries run. A pool added with `db.pool(name)` returns the same error from every call until a check passes.
>
> **What it does.** One query over the catalog, on a pool's first connection, covering every model in the binary, and nothing after: no work on later connections or queries. 200 tables took about 3 ms on a local connection. Every pool runs it, replicas included, so a replica that hasn't replayed a migration yet fails it until it has. It works behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, checking the database PgBouncer connects you to.
>
> ```toml
> [pools.legacy]
> check_schema = "off"     # this database holds none of this binary's models
> ```
>
> **When it's right.** Only for a pool whose database isn't meant to hold the binary's models, such as a pool used only for raw SQL on another database. `MORM_POOL_CHECK_SCHEMA=off` does the same for the pool a process opens at startup. Never turn it off to get a failing build to start: the check failed because that build can't use this schema.
>
> **What you give up.** A build brought back after a migration's `contract`, such as a rollback of the app to an older release, starts anyway, and Postgres changes what it writes with no error: a field built for a wider scale, timestamp precision or length than its column stores `1.0051` as `1.01` or `'abc  '` as `'abc'`. A missing column or an unrelated type fails each query that reaches it, in production, instead of failing at startup. `db.check_schema()` still runs the check whenever you call it.

reqs.text: **What changes together.** A type change on a column that a foreign key references, where the table has to be rewritten or the column's collation changes, and the old and new types are in the same one of the type families step 41's `check_schema` accepts, runs online by default in this form, in either direction. That's every such change within one family, not only between `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`: an `integer` primary key becoming `bigint` or going back, an `integer` key becoming `numeric(20,0)`, a `numeric(20,4)` key becoming `numeric(20,2)`, a `varchar(10)` key becoming `varchar(3)`, or a `char(3)` key becoming `char(5)`. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, the table's file changed for a change of `numeric` scale, a lower `numeric` precision, `numeric(10,0)` to `bigint` or `numeric(8,0)`, `integer` to `bigint` or `numeric(12,0)`, a lower timestamp precision, a shorter `varchar`, `text` to `varchar(n)`, every change of a `char` length, longer included, and every array change, such as `int[]` to `bigint[]` or `varchar(5)[]` to `text[]`. It stayed the same for a higher `numeric` precision at the same scale or unbounded `numeric`, a higher timestamp precision, and a longer `varchar` or `text`. So a `char` or array key reaches this form even when it gets longer, and so does every narrowing that rewrites. The group is every column of the changed key, plus every column that references it, followed transitively: a referencing column that is itself referenced brings its own referencing columns in. The group also includes the identity or owned sequence, every index and constraint on those columns, and the views and materialized views over them, carried as step 39 carries them. A composite key changes only the columns whose type changes, and keeps its other columns in each index and foreign key. A self-referencing table gets a shadow column for the key and one for the referencing column, with one sync trigger. A referencing column whose type doesn't change, such as a `bigint` column referencing an `integer` key that becomes `bigint`, stays in the group with no shadow column, and step 5's new foreign key starts from that column itself. Step 06's typed foreign keys make the models change every referencing column with the key, so the diff shows the whole group, and the planner makes it one op. A widening that needs no rewrite, such as a longer `varchar` or a higher precision on `numeric(p,0)`, stays step 39's change in place, and a change across families, such as `integer` to `uuid`, or `timestamp` to `timestamptz`, keeps step 39's refusal on a live table, with `--fast`.

reqs.text:
**The steps,** each with its own boundary, and each brief lock taken under `lock_timeout` with retries, as step 33 says:

1. `tx` per table, the key table first: add a shadow column for each changed column, with its new type and its collation named, as step 39 does, and one sync trigger, `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE`, that copies each old column into its shadow. `ADD COLUMN` takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` and `CREATE TRIGGER` takes `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE`, each for under a millisecond.
2. `batch` per table: copy by the table's copy key, as R-1148 says, up to its bound, the highest key read once that table's trigger has committed, as step 52's copy does, with the cursor in `_morm.steps`.
3. `no-tx`: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for each primary key or unique index that holds a changed column, and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for every other index that holds one, each with the shadow column in place of the old one, so a composite key keeps its other columns. Each new index is named `_morm_new_<name>`, from the real index's name through the 63-byte name function, so step 14 maps a unique violation on a shadow index to the key's field.
4. `tx`, then a separate `tx`: add a `CHECK ... NOT VALID` on each shadow column, then `VALIDATE` it. The check is `(new IS NOT DISTINCT FROM CAST(old AS <new type>))`, with `new IS NOT NULL AND` in front for a `NOT NULL` old column, and for a type with a collation the cast side names the new column's collation, as `CAST(old AS <new type>) COLLATE "<collation>"`. That's one rule for every change: `new = old` can never pass where the values change, as `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)` showed when it failed `VALIDATE` on 200,000 rows, and doesn't exist between arrays of different types. Any other CHECK naming a changed column is added on its shadow column `NOT VALID` and validated the same way. `VALIDATE` takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE`, so writes carry on.
5. `tx`, then a separate `tx`, for each foreign key that references a changed column: lock the referenced table `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE`, then add the new foreign key on the shadow columns, or on a referencing column whose type doesn't change, `REFERENCES` the referenced table's shadow columns, with the same actions, `MATCH` type and deferrability, `NOT VALID`. Then `VALIDATE` it, which takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` on the referencing table and `ROW SHARE` on the referenced one, so writes carry on.
6. `no-tx`: `ANALYZE` the shadow columns.
7. `tx` per materialized view above the group: build it beside the old one, as late as possible, as step 39 does.
8. `tx`: the cutover, as R-1123 says.

Each index and CHECK on a shadow column takes its text from Postgres, by the route steps 39 and 52 use. Step 4's check proves two things in one scan: every row was copied, and with the value the cast gives, which is the value the sync trigger's assignment gives every row it stores. The cast depends only on the value, so a key and its references change alike. It also lets Postgres skip the scan when the cutover sets `NOT NULL` or adds the primary key, which `CHECK (new = old)` alone doesn't: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, the cast form validated on a key table and a referencing table going from `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)`, `SET NOT NULL` logged that existing constraints were sufficient to prove the column holds no nulls, and `ADD PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` worked. Step 5 waits for every copy and for step 3, because a key that isn't copied yet would fail the new foreign key's checks on app writes. The new foreign key references the shadow columns' unique index before that index becomes the primary key, which Postgres allows, and the cutover turns that same index into the key, so the foreign key stays tied to it. Step 5 takes the referenced table's lock before the referencing table's, because the other order waited on app transactions for hundreds of attempts.

reqs.text:
**The cutover** is one short transaction across every table in the group, and it gives way to live transactions under step 39's rule, with the same settings, the same `--terminate-blockers` and the same `--resume`. In order:

1. Take each carried view's lock with its own `DROP VIEW`, from the outside in, as step 39 does. Then lock the tables `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`: the key table first, then the referencing tables in name order. Readers, and writers going from a parent to its children, lock the key table first, and under nonstop traffic a cutover that locked the referencing tables first got in on none of 176 attempts.
2. Walk the group again under the lock, reading `pg_constraint` for every foreign key that references a changed column. Anything new stops the cutover with nothing changed.
3. Take the sequence's lock with a same-value `ALTER SEQUENCE ... INCREMENT BY <current>`, because `LOCK TABLE` refuses a sequence, then read `last_value` and `is_called`.
4. Drop the sync triggers and the old foreign keys.
5. On each table: drop the identity, which drops its sequence, the old primary key or unique constraints and the other old indexes on the changed columns. Retire each old column as step 38 does, dropping its `NOT NULL` and default and renaming it to its retired name. Rename each shadow column to the real name, then `SET NOT NULL` where the old column had it, which the validated check proves with no scan, and set the old column's default. Re-attach the primary key with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` and each unique constraint with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> UNIQUE USING INDEX`, then carry the sequence as R-1124 says.
6. Drop the checks, and rename the new foreign keys and indexes to the real names. Move a `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on a replaced index to its new index, because dropping the old one leaves the table with no replica identity index.
7. Recreate the carried views and swap the materialized views, as step 39 does, refresh functions, as step 37 does, copy column comments and grants, and write the step as `done` in `_morm.steps`, all in this same transaction.

It holds `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on every table in the group, `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` and then `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` on the sequence, and each carried view's lock. Everything inside it is a catalog change, with no scan and no rewrite.

reqs.text: **The sequence.** An identity key keeps its sequence's name and position. Once the shadow column has the real name, the cutover runs `ADD GENERATED ALWAYS` or `BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (SEQUENCE NAME <old name>, <old options>)`, the same kind as before, with the old start, increment, cache and cycle, and with a minimum or maximum the old sequence set past its type's default. A minimum or maximum that was the old type's default becomes the new type's, so an `integer` identity widened to `bigint` can reach `bigint`'s maximum. Then `setval` sets the `last_value` and `is_called` read under the lock. The new sequence doesn't keep the old one's owner, grants or comment, so the cutover copies them. A session open across the cutover gets `55000` from `currval` and `lastval` on that sequence until its next `nextval`, because the sequence is new under the same name, and the README says so. A `serial` key, with an owned sequence and no identity, keeps the same sequence, with its OID and position: `ALTER SEQUENCE ... AS <new type>` changes its type, moving a maximum that was the old type's default to the new type's and keeping one set explicitly, and `OWNED BY` and `SET DEFAULT` move it to the new column. Postgres allows identity, and sequences, only on `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, so all of this holds within those three types, and R-1125 refuses an op that takes a generated key out of them while dropping its generation. A `serial` key's `ALTER SEQUENCE ... AS` runs only when its new type is one of the three. A `serial` key moved to `numeric(p,0)` with its `nextval` default kept keeps its sequence as it was, with `OWNED BY` and `SET DEFAULT` moved to the new column, and on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11 one did keep working, with its sequence still `integer`. Its position is checked as R-1127 says, because a `numeric(5,0)` key with a `nextval` default got `numeric field overflow` on the insert after its sequence passed 99,999.

reqs.text:
**Refused online, with the evidence.** Each of these is refused with exit code `2` before the op's first step, changing nothing. `makemigrations` checks what scratch shows, `migrate` and `rollback` preflight check the live database, and the cutover's second walk checks again under its lock, where anything new stops it with nothing changed.

1. A foreign key on a changed column from a table no model declares, or one the models don't declare. The evidence is the referencing table, the constraint's name and `pg_get_constraintdef`, its deferrability and the table's estimated rows. morm can't change a column it doesn't manage, and if that column stayed narrow, its foreign key would fail once a value passed the old limit. It's a refusal, not a decision, because no answer would make the change safe. The fix is to declare the table in the models, or to drop that foreign key first. `--fast` refuses it too, as R-1126 says. The cutover's `DROP CONSTRAINT`, which never uses `CASCADE`, is the last check, because Postgres refuses to drop a key a foreign key needs, with `2BP01`.
2. A partitioned table or a partition in the group, because `ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX` isn't supported on a partitioned table, Postgres 15 to 17 can't add a `NOT VALID` foreign key from one, and Postgres can't add a column to a partition. `--fast` handles it when every partition the change reaches is declared by a model with the same change, as R-1126 says.
3. A table in the group that's in any publication, or is a subscription's target, naming the publication or subscription, because the shadow columns and the cutover each stop replication with `missing replicated column`. `--fast` handles it, and the subscriber keeps working.
4. What step 52 refuses for an enum swap, on a column in the group: exclusion constraints and extended statistics, stored generated columns that read one, a domain or composite type, and a view or materialized view that would still read the retired column once recreated, such as `SELECT *`. Each of these needs a rewrite, or a definition morm can't move with no lock. `--fast` handles them.
5. Anything step 39 refuses above a swapped column, such as a view no model declares.
6. A table in the group that's in old-style inheritance, as a parent or as a child, naming the table and its parent or children, because `ADD COLUMN` on a parent adds the column to every child, `ALTER TABLE ONLY` can't stop that, and an inherited column's type can't change on the child alone. `--fast` handles it when every child the change reaches is declared by a model with the same change, as R-1126 says.
7. A table in the group with no primary key and no unique `NOT NULL` key, naming the table, because its copy has no key to bound it or resume it by, as R-1148 says. `--fast` handles it.
8. A referencing column whose new type is in a different btree operator family from the key's new type, naming both columns, such as a `bigint` column referencing a key that becomes `numeric(20,0)`. Postgres allows that foreign key, but compares through a cast, so it can't use the referencing column's index: deleting 10 keys took 683 ms on 18.6 and 668 ms on 17.11, with a parallel sequential scan of the referencing table filtered on `(pid)::numeric`, against 2 ms with matching types. `--fast` refuses it too.
9. When the change alters stored values, as R-1149 says, a referencing column that doesn't take exactly the key's new type, naming it, because a reference left at the old scale would no longer match its key. `--fast` refuses it too.
10. One op that takes a generated key, an identity column or a `serial` key with its owned sequence, out of `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint` while dropping its generation, naming the column. Postgres allows identity and sequences only on those types: on 18.6 and 17.11, `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE numeric(20,0)` on an identity column, the `ADD GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` this op's cutover would run on a `numeric` column, and `CREATE TABLE` with a `numeric` identity column each failed with `identity column type must be smallint, integer, or bigint`, and `CREATE SEQUENCE ... AS numeric` failed with `sequence type must be smallint, integer, or bigint`. So no sequence can count past `bigint`'s maximum, and a generated key gains no room as `numeric`. `--fast` refuses it too, because Postgres can't do it either. The way through is two migrations: the first drops the identity or the default, which changes no rows, and the second changes the type, with no sequence involved. `DROP IDENTITY` keeps the data and drops the sequence, and step 41 refuses at pool start a build that still leaves that column out of its inserts.
11. A collation change on a key with a nondeterministic collation on either side, naming both collations, because it can merge keys, as `'abc'` and `'ABC'` did when a key went from `"C"` to a case-insensitive collation, and Postgres refuses a foreign key between two different collations when either is nondeterministic. Between two deterministic collations, equality is byte equality, so nothing merges, and the change runs online. `--fast` handles it, as R-1126 says, and a merge there fails on the unique index and changes nothing.

An enum key keeps step 52's refusal, because an enum swap isn't a change within one family.

reqs.text: **The inverse, for `rollback` and `revert`,** runs this form in the other direction, online, and so does a migration that narrows a referenced key within one family. The retired columns become the shadow columns again: a sync trigger from the new columns to the old, a full copy, because rows changed since the cutover need it too, the indexes, checks and foreign keys, then a cutover that renames back and moves the identity back to a sequence of the old type. reqs.text: **Recovery.** Each step has a precondition, so `--resume` carries on from the boundary where it stopped. A rerun of steps 1 and 3 to 5 reads the catalog first and does only what's missing. A concurrent index left `indisvalid = false` is dropped and built again, a constraint left `NOT VALID` is validated again, and the copy resumes from its cursor. The cutover is one transaction, so a process killed inside it changes nothing, and a rerun starts it again. `rollback --failed` drops the shadow objects, which are the sync triggers, shadow columns, new indexes, checks and foreign keys, and leaves the old columns, keys and sequence in place.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **Changing a key other tables reference can be refused.** A type change on a key that foreign keys reference, such as an `integer` primary key becoming `bigint`, or any other change within one kind of type that rewrites the table, such as `numeric(20,4)` becoming `numeric(20,2)`, runs online with apps up. morm changes every column that references the key, and the identity sequence, with it. It adds a new column beside each one, copies the rows in batches, builds the indexes and foreign keys with no long lock, and swaps them all in one cutover of milliseconds. `rollback` and `revert` go back the same way.
>
> **What it refuses, and how to go on.** In these cases morm stops the migration with exit code `2`, naming the cause, before it changes anything:
>
> - **A foreign key your models don't declare,** on a table they don't declare or on one they do. morm can't change a column it doesn't manage, and if that column stayed narrow, its foreign key would fail once an id passed the old limit. `--fast` refuses it too. Declare the table in your models, or drop that foreign key first.
> - **A partitioned table, a partition, a table in old-style inheritance, or a table in a publication or a subscription.** Postgres can't swap a partitioned table's key without a scan, a new column on an inheritance parent lands on every child, and the new columns would stop replication. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead. On a partitioned or inherited table, `--fast` needs every partition and child declared in your models with the same change, as the notice on inherited columns says.
> - **A table with no primary key and no unique key on `NOT NULL` columns.** The copy has no key to walk by. Add one first, or run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **An exclusion constraint, extended statistics, a stored generated column, a domain or composite type, or a view such as `SELECT *`, on a column in the change, or a view your models don't declare.** morm can't move these with no lock. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **A change to another kind of type,** such as `integer` to `uuid`, or `timestamp` to `timestamptz`. Run `makemigrations --fast` instead.
> - **A generated key leaving the integer types, a reference of another kind of number, keys that would merge, and some collation changes.** The notices below say why, and how to go on.
> - **Going back down,** such as a `rollback` from `bigint` to `integer`, **once a value or the sequence has passed the old type's limit.** Nothing makes that safe, so nothing forces it. Leave the column wide, or remove the values that don't fit first.
>
> **When `--fast` is right.** Only with apps stopped, in a maintenance window, or on tables small enough that a full lock for their rewrite doesn't matter.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites each table under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on any of them waits until it's done, and `max_rewrite_mb` refuses a table bigger than its limit. Going back down online, an app write the old type can't hold, such as a new id past `2^31 - 1`, fails with `22003` from the migration's first step, not only after the cutover.

reqs.text: The README says this plainly, beside that notice. When an identity key's type changes online, the cutover replaces its sequence with a new one under the same name, at the same position. A session that was open across the cutover gets `55000` from `currval` and `lastval` on that sequence until it next calls `nextval`, such as with its next insert. So read a new id from `RETURNING`, not from `currval` or `lastval`. A `serial` key keeps its sequence, so it isn't affected.

So `makemigrations` opens a decision for each column that changes between the two, in either direction, naming the table, the column and both types, and asking which zone the stored values are in. The online swap's copy and sync trigger convert through the same zone, and the down converts back through it. On a key that foreign keys reference, this change is across families, so it's refused on a live table and `--fast` runs it, as R-0567 says.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the cutover settings:

> **A cutover that takes many locks can be refused before it starts.** A cutover gives way to your app: each lock waits at most `cutover_lock_timeout`, and then the attempt changes nothing and tries again, so Postgres never has to kill one of your transactions to break a deadlock. Postgres starts looking for a deadlock once a lock has waited `deadlock_timeout`, and an attempt holds every lock it has while it waits for the next, so morm shrinks each lock's wait to `deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks)` when that's shorter, and says so. Postgres counts `lock_timeout` in whole milliseconds and reads 0 as no limit, so when that wait comes to under 1 ms, `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before the change's first step, naming `cutover_lock_timeout`, `deadlock_timeout` and the number of locks, and change nothing.
>
> **How to go on.** Raise `deadlock_timeout` on the server, so each lock gets at least a millisecond: its default of `1s` covers a cutover of up to 500 locks. If `cutover_lock_timeout` is the one set under 1 ms, raise that instead. Or write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window.
>
> **What you give up.** With a higher `deadlock_timeout`, a real deadlock between your own transactions takes that long to be broken. `--fast` changes the tables in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An online change needs a key to walk the table.** When morm changes a column's type online, swaps an enum online, or changes a key other tables reference, it copies the rows in batches, walking the table by its primary key, so the copy stops at a fixed point and carries on after a crash. A table with no primary key is walked by a unique key whose columns are all `NOT NULL`, with no `WHERE` and no expression. A table with neither is refused before anything changes, with exit code `2`, naming the table.
>
> **How to go on.** Add a primary key, or a unique key on `NOT NULL` columns, in an earlier migration, or write this one with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites the table in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on it waits until it's done.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A generated key stays an integer.** Postgres allows identity columns, and sequences, only on `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, and no sequence can count past `bigint`'s maximum, so a generated key gains nothing as `numeric`. So `identity` on any other type is a compile error, and a migration that takes a key out of the integer types while dropping its identity, or a `serial` key's sequence, is refused with exit code `2` when it's made.
>
> **When it's right to go there anyway.** When your app supplies its own ids, such as `u64` ids from another system, stored as `numeric(20,0)`.
>
> **How to go on.** Use two migrations. The first drops the identity, or the default, which changes no rows. The second changes the type, with no sequence involved.
>
> **What you give up.** The database no longer makes the ids, so every insert must supply one, and a build that still leaves the id out of its inserts is refused when its pool starts. If you add identity back later, morm sets its sequence past the highest key, so the next insert doesn't collide.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **Changing a key's values changes them everywhere.** A key change that lowers a scale, a timestamp precision or a length, such as `numeric(20,4)` to `numeric(20,2)`, changes the stored keys: `1.0051` becomes `1.01`. morm runs it online and changes every column that references the key the same way, so no reference is lost. Like every change Postgres would round or cut silently, it waits for `migrate --phase contract`, or for `--fast` with apps stopped. `makemigrations` asks you to accept it as a `lossy` decision, naming every referencing column, and `migrate` asks again with the number of rows that would change.
>
> **What it refuses.** Two keys that would become one, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149`, both `1.01`, stop `migrate` or `rollback` with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming them, because no answer can make two keys one. A referencing column that doesn't change to exactly the key's new type is refused when the migration is made, because it would no longer match its key.
>
> **How to go on.** Change or remove the keys that would merge, then run it again.
>
> **What you give up.** Copies of the key held outside the database, such as in caches, URLs, other services, logs and exports, keep the old values and won't match any more. While it runs, a write whose key matches another only once rounded fails with `Error::Unique` on the key's field.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A narrower key is refused while a value doesn't fit.** Going down to a narrower key, by `rollback`, `revert` or a narrowing migration, such as `bigint` to `integer` or `varchar(10)` to `varchar(3)`, stops with exit code `2` before anything changes when a live value doesn't fit the narrower type, naming the table, the column, one such value and how many there are. A sequence past the narrower limit is refused the same way. Nothing makes that safe, so nothing forces it.
>
> From the migration's first step until it's done, a write the narrower type can't hold fails with the database's error for that write, such as `22003` for an id past `2^31 - 1` or `22001` for a text too long. A row that doesn't fit and arrives before the migration's trigger is in place stops the copy with the same message, and `rollback --failed` cleans up.
>
> **How to go on.** Leave the key wide, or change or remove the values that don't fit first.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **A reference must stay the key's kind of number.** When a key changes, every column that references it must end up the same kind of type as the key. Postgres accepts a `bigint` column referencing a `numeric(20,0)` key, but compares the two through a cast, so the foreign key can't use the referencing column's index, and every delete of a key reads the whole referencing table: deleting 10 keys took 683 ms, against 2 ms with matching types. So `makemigrations` refuses it with exit code `2`, naming both columns, with `--fast` too.
>
> **How to go on.** Give the referencing column the key's new type.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **Some collation changes on a key are refused online.** morm names a column's collation in every type change it writes, because Postgres would otherwise reset it to the default, and a collation change on its own runs through the online swap, because it rebuilds the column's indexes. A key whose collation changes between two deterministic collations, where equal means the same bytes, changes online like any other key change. A change to or from a nondeterministic collation, such as a case-insensitive one, is refused online with exit code `2`, naming both collations, because it can turn two keys into one, such as `'abc'` and `'ABC'`, and Postgres won't keep a foreign key between the two collations while the change runs.
>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it with apps stopped. If two keys would become one, it fails on the unique index and changes nothing.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` rewrites every table in the change in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **A change between `timestamp` and `timestamptz` asks which zone your values are in.** Postgres converts each value through the time zone of the session that runs the change, with no error, so the same stored `12:00` becomes `12:00` UTC on one host and `17:00` UTC on another. So `makemigrations` stops with exit code `3` and asks which zone the stored values are in, then writes that zone into the migration, so it gives the same data wherever it runs, and its down converts back through the same zone.
>
> **How to answer.** `makemigrations --decide ID=<zone>`, such as `ID=UTC`, with the zone your app wrote the values in.
>
> **What you give up.** One zone covers every row of the column, so rows written in different zones need fixing first. On a key other tables reference, the change can't run online, so it needs `makemigrations --fast`.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the notice on changing a key other tables reference:

> **`--fast` on a key rebuilds its foreign keys and indexes.** With `--fast`, a key change that changes stored values, moves to another kind of number, such as `integer` to `numeric(20,0)`, or changes to or from a nondeterministic collation can't run with the foreign keys in place. So morm drops the foreign keys on the key, changes every column, and adds them back with the same names and rules, checking every row, all in the one transaction. Then it rebuilds any index on those columns that Postgres changed on its own, such as one whose operator class it replaced, so every index ends as your models declare it.
>
> **What you give up.** All of this runs under the one full lock, so checking the foreign keys and rebuilding the indexes adds to the time every read and write on those tables waits.

**Key values that change.** A key change that's one of step 41's silent narrowings, a lower scale, a lower timestamp precision or a shorter length that drops trailing spaces, changes stored keys, such as `1.0051` to `1.01`, and runs in this form, held for `contract` as step 41 holds every silent narrowing, or under `--fast` as R-1126 says. A `char` key that gets shorter changes no value, because Postgres compares `char` without its padding. Step 4's cast check passes where `new = old` can't, and a key and its references round alike. Before the op's first step, `migrate` and `rollback` preflight refuse with exit code `2` any key values that would merge, naming them, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149`, which both become `1.01`, with one `GROUP BY` per key, built from the new type, in a read-only transaction with `statement_timeout` off. The same check runs for every other unique index that holds a changed column, such as one on a single column of a composite key, where two keys can stay distinct while that column's values merge, built as step 39 builds it for its swap, naming the table, the index, the values and how many rows hold each. No answer can make two keys one, so it's a refusal, not a decision. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a merge made `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` fail with `Key (id_new)=(1.01) is duplicated` and left the index invalid, `timestamp` to `timestamp(3)` merged `.123456` with `.123`, `varchar(10)` to `varchar(3)` merged `'abc  '` with `'abc'`, and `--fast` failed the same way. A merge written after preflight fails step 3's unique index build, and the step stops as `failed`. Every referencing column must take exactly the key's new type, as R-1125 says, and step 41 words the `lossy` decision and its live counts for a key. During the window, a write whose key collides with another only once rounded fails on the shadow unique index, and step 14 maps that index's name to the key's field, so the error reads as one on the key. In `contract`, apps are built for the narrower shape, and step 13 stops them writing extra decimals, so this is rare.

Measured on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11: a key table of 300,000 `numeric(20,4)` primary keys, each ending `.0051`, referenced by 400,000 `NOT NULL` rows with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, went to `numeric(20,2)` through steps 1 to 6 and the cutover, run by hand with the cast check and the key table locked first. 8 `pgbench` clients ran nonstop, writing two-decimal keys: inserting a parent and a child, deleting by key range with its cascade, updating a parent and then reading its children, moving a child to another parent, and a join. On 18.6, 89,098 transactions ran and none failed, the copies took 61 and 81 bounded batches, and the cutover got in on attempt 3, holding its locks for 8.3 ms. On 17.11, 74,116 ran and none failed, with the same batches, and the cutover got in on attempt 2 at 7.0 ms. On both, no row was orphaned, every parent's new key was its old key rounded, every child whose key differed from its retired one had moved to another parent after the cutover, and the tables ended `numeric(20,2)`, with `parent_pkey` and `child_pid_fkey` on the new columns and no trigger left. Each was a single short run with no fault injection, which T-0230 and T-0231 add.

reqs.text:
**Checking that a value fits a narrower type.** R-1127's check covers every narrowing in this form that raises a real error on a value that doesn't fit, in any family, because the silent ones change values instead, as R-1149 says. A write's assignment cast is the authority, and `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, `UPDATE ... SET` and a plpgsql trigger's `NEW.x := NEW.y` all use it. An explicit `CAST` isn't, because `CAST('abcd' AS varchar(3))` gives `'abc'` with no error, while assigning `'abcd'` to a `varchar(3)` fails with `22001`. reqs.text: **Indexes after a type change.** `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` rebuilds a column's indexes from their stored definitions without checking them against the models: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11 it silently swapped an explicit `int4_ops` for `bigint`'s default class and kept `varchar_pattern_ops` on a column changed to `text`, so an index could end unlike the models with no error. So every `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` morm writes, in place, under `--fast`, in a `down.sql` or in a later step's one-transaction form, is followed by one shared check. Once the change has run on scratch, `makemigrations` reads `pg_get_indexdef` for each index on that table that holds a changed column, compares it with the definition the target schema builds on scratch, the models' for an up and the chain's before the migration for a down, and the migration recreates each that differs from the target's definition. Under `--fast` and in a one-transaction form, it's dropped and created again in the same transaction, right after the change, under the lock that transaction already holds. In place on a live table, it's rebuilt as R-0319 says, with no long lock: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, or `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for a unique one, under the name `_morm_new_<name>`, made from its name `<name>` through the 63-byte name function, then `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on the old one and a rename to `<name>`, and a build left `indisvalid = false` is dropped and built again on `--resume`. An index that a primary key or unique constraint owns can't be dropped on its own, so in one short transaction that gives way under R-1072's rule, its constraint is dropped and attached again to the new index with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` or `UNIQUE USING INDEX`, which takes no scan, because the columns keep their `NOT NULL`. An index a foreign key references is rebuilt as R-1158 says, and one on a partitioned table as R-1160 says. An index that matches is left alone. Nothing is dropped with `CASCADE`. An `ops` that doesn't accept the new type fails the target's build on scratch, naming the index and its `ops`, as `operator class "int4_ops" does not accept data type bigint`, so `makemigrations` writes no file. The online swap runs no `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE`, and builds its indexes from scratch's definitions, as R-1153 says. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An online change refuses partitioned and inherited tables.** When morm changes a column's type or collation online, swaps an enum online, or changes a key other tables reference, it adds a new column beside the old one, copies the rows, builds the indexes with no long lock, and renames them at cutover. Postgres can't do that on a partitioned table or a partition: it can't build an index concurrently on a partitioned table, or add a column to a partition. On a table in old-style inheritance, a new column on a parent lands on every child, and an inherited column's type can't change on a child alone. So `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the table and its partitions, parent or children.
>
> **How to go on.** Write the migration with `makemigrations --fast` and run it in a maintenance window. On a partitioned table or an inheritance parent, Postgres changes the column on every partition and child with it, so morm runs it only when your models declare every one of them with the same change, as the notice on inherited columns says.
>
> **When `--fast` is right.** Only with apps stopped, or on tables small enough that a full lock for their rewrite doesn't matter.
>
> **What you give up.** `--fast` changes the column in one transaction under `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, on every partition and child too, so every read and write on them waits until it's done.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **A type change rebuilds an index Postgres changed on its own, and stops on one that can't fit.** `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` rebuilds a column's indexes from their old definitions without checking them against your models: it silently replaced an explicit `int4_ops` with `bigint`'s default class, and kept `varchar_pattern_ops` on a column changed to `text`. So after every type change, in place, under `--fast` or in an enum swap, morm compares each index on the column with what your models build on scratch and rebuilds any that differs: in place on a live table with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, and under `--fast` in the same transaction. An online swap builds its new indexes from your models in the first place. An index whose `ops` doesn't accept the new type stops `makemigrations`, naming the index and its `ops`, such as `operator class "int4_ops" does not accept data type bigint`.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: an index whose class doesn't accept the new type can't exist on it, so there's no override.
>
> **How to go on.** Change that index's `ops` in your model to one for the new type, or remove it to use the type's default class, then run `makemigrations` again.
>
> **What you give up.** Under `--fast`, a rebuild adds to the time every read and write on that table waits. In place, the new index is built beside the old one, so it takes the time and space of a fresh index. While it builds, and while an online swap runs, a write whose value matches another row's only once converted, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149` both becoming `1.01`, fails with `Error::Unique` on the column's field.

reqs.text: **Inherited columns.** Postgres changes an inherited column only through the table it comes from. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` on a child's or a partition's inherited column alone failed with `cannot alter inherited column`, and so did a collation change, while the same change on the top parent changed it on every child, grandchild and partition. `ALTER TABLE ONLY` on the parent was refused with `type of inherited column ... must be changed in child tables too`, and a column a child inherits from two parents couldn't be changed from either, each failing with `cannot alter inherited column ... of relation`. So every `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE` morm runs, in place, under `--fast`, in a `down.sql` or in a later step's one-transaction form, changes an inherited column only through its top parent, in one `ALTER`. Scratch is built from the models, so it has no inheritance, and `migrate` and `rollback` preflight read `pg_inherits` and `pg_attribute` on the live database for every column the migration changes. A column on a table with children or partitions, or one a table inherits, changes only when the migration makes the same change, to the same type and collation, on its top parent and on every child and partition the change reaches, each declared by a model. Then preflight runs the top parent's step where the first step in that tree sits. That step takes the top parent's lock, reads `pg_inherits` again and stops with nothing changed if the tree has changed since preflight, then runs the one `ALTER`. Each other step in the tree finds by its precondition that its column already has the new type and collation, so it changes nothing apart from R-1152's check on its own table. Otherwise preflight refuses with exit code `2` before the first step, changing nothing, naming the column, its top parent and every child and partition the change reaches: a change to a child's or a partition's inherited column without the same change on its top parent, a change that would reach a child or a partition no model declares or whose model doesn't make the same change, and a change to a column inherited from more than one parent, which no one `ALTER` can make. morm never changes a table it doesn't manage, and Postgres would change such a child with no model asking for it. The message says to declare every child and partition in the models with the same change. A column a child adds of its own isn't inherited, so it changes on that child like a column of any other table.

**Foreign keys on a rebuilt index.** A foreign key depends on the unique index it references, so Postgres won't drop that index, or the primary key or unique constraint that owns it, while the foreign key is there. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a `varchar(10)` key with a unique index on `varchar_pattern_ops`, referenced by a foreign key, kept that class when changed in place to `text`, and `DROP INDEX` failed with `cannot drop index ... because other objects depend on it`, and `DROP CONSTRAINT` on a referenced primary key with `2BP01`. A foreign key added beside the old one, `NOT VALID`, with a column list or without, was tied to the old index, not to a new one built beside it, so Postgres gives no way to move a foreign key to a new index while the old one is there. So when R-1152's check must rebuild an index that a foreign key references, morm drops and adds back each such foreign key around the rebuild, in every form, never with `CASCADE`. Under `--fast` and in a one-transaction form, in the same transaction: it drops them, drops and creates the index again, attaching its primary key or unique constraint to it, and adds them back, validated, under the lock it already holds. In place on a live table, with no long lock and no moment when a row that breaks a foreign key could be written:

1. `no-tx`: build the new index as R-1152 says, under `_morm_new_<name>`.
2. `tx`: one short transaction that gives way to live transactions under R-1072's rule, with its settings, its scaled wait and `--terminate-blockers`. Lock the referenced table `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, then each referencing table in name order, drop the foreign keys, drop the old index or its constraint, rename the new index to `<name>`, attaching a primary key or unique constraint to it with `ADD CONSTRAINT <name> PRIMARY KEY USING INDEX` or `UNIQUE USING INDEX`, and add each foreign key back with its name, columns, actions, `MATCH` type and deferrability, `NOT VALID`. Every statement is a catalog change, with no scan.
3. `tx` per foreign key: `VALIDATE`, which takes `SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE` on the referencing table and `ROW SHARE` on the referenced one, so writes carry on.

reqs.text: **Values that would merge on a unique index.** A swap's conversion can make two values equal, such as `1.0051` and `1.0149` both becoming `1.01` in `numeric(10,2)`, `'01'` and `'1'` both becoming `1` from `text` to `integer`, `'abc'` and `'ABC'` under a case-insensitive collation, or `02:30` and `03:30` on the day clocks go forward, both becoming the same `timestamptz`. On a unique index that holds the column, R-1153's concurrent build would then fail mid-run and leave the index invalid. So before R-0566's swap changes anything, it runs one `GROUP BY` for each unique index that holds a swapped column, in a read-only transaction with `statement_timeout` off, and refuses with exit code `2` any values that would merge, naming the table, the index, the values and how many rows hold each. No answer can make two rows one, so it's a refusal, not a decision. The query is built with no SQL parser. Its keys and predicate are the shadow index's, read on scratch with `pg_get_indexdef` and `pg_get_expr` as R-1153 reads them, and it reads from a subquery that adds the shadow column under its own name, with the value the copy gives it: the cast with its collation, the migration's `USING`, or R-1135's zone. A row with a null in any key is left out, unless the index is `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`. `migrate` and `rollback` preflight run it. When the new type doesn't exist yet, because the migration creates it, as every enum swap's does, preflight runs it in a transaction of its own, with `statement_timeout` off, that first runs the migration's statements creating that type, then the `GROUP BY`, and always rolls back. So a merge is a preflight refusal with exit code `2`, with nothing recorded and no migration left `failed`, as for any other type. `CREATE TYPE` is transactional, so the rollback leaves no type behind, and the transaction takes only `ACCESS SHARE` on the table and its indexes, and on the schema and the old type: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, with it held open after the `GROUP BY` had found a merge, an `UPDATE`, an `INSERT`, a `DELETE`, and `ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE` on the old type, from another session with a `500ms` `lock_timeout`, each went through, and after the rollback `pg_type` held no new type. It's skipped only for a change between `smallint`, `integer` and `bigint`, where each value keeps its number or fails with an error. A merge written after the check fails the concurrent unique build, which stops that step as `failed`, and `rollback --failed` drops the shadow objects. Until cutover, a write that would merge gets `Error::Unique` on the shadow index, as R-1153 says. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, this query found `1.01` twice for `numeric(10,4)` to `numeric(10,2)`, the same `(1, 1)` twice on a partial two-column unique index for `text` to `integer`, rows outside its predicate left out, and `abc` twice for a change to a case-insensitive ICU collation, with the nulls left out, while building the same unique index concurrently on the copied values failed with `could not create unique index` and left it invalid. Both `America/New_York` times above gave the same `timestamptz`, and so did `01:30` before and after clocks went back, going the other way.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **An inherited column changes only through its top parent.** On a partitioned table, or a table in old-style inheritance, a column the children inherit can only be changed on the table at the top. Postgres refuses to change it on a child or a partition alone, with `cannot alter inherited column`, and a change on the top parent changes it on every child and partition with it. So when a migration changes such a column's type or collation, `migrate` and `rollback` run one `ALTER` on the top parent, and only when your models declare every child and partition it reaches, each with the same change. Otherwise they stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the column, its top parent and every child and partition: a change to a child's or a partition's column without its top parent, a change that would reach a child or a partition your models don't declare, or declare with the old type, and a change to a column a child inherits from two parents, which no one `ALTER` can make.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: morm never changes a table your models don't declare, and Postgres can't change a child's inherited column on its own.
>
> **How to go on.** Declare every child and partition in your models with the same change, make it on the top parent too, and run `makemigrations` again. A column a child inherits from two parents can't be changed by morm, so change it by hand outside morm, then let your models follow.
>
> **What you give up.** A child or a partition you'd rather leave out of your models has to be declared before its inherited column can change.

The README shows this notice loudly, beside the online swap:

> **A type change drops and adds back the foreign keys on an index it rebuilds.** When morm rebuilds an index after a type change, as the notice above says, and a foreign key references that index, Postgres won't drop the index while the foreign key is there, and has no way to move the foreign key to a new index. So morm drops the foreign key and adds it back with the same name and rules. In place on a live table, it builds the new index first with no long lock, swaps the index and the foreign keys in one short transaction that gives way to your app, as a cutover does, and then checks the existing rows with `VALIDATE`, which doesn't block writes. Every write is checked by the old foreign key or the new one, so no row that breaks it can get in. Under `--fast`, all of it runs in the one transaction. A foreign key your models don't declare on that index stops the migration with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming it.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: the index can't be rebuilt any other way.
>
> **How to go on.** For a foreign key your models don't declare, declare its table in your models, or drop that foreign key first.
>
> **What you give up.** The short transaction takes a full lock on the key table and every table that references it, for a few milliseconds. Until `VALIDATE` finishes, Postgres marks the foreign key `NOT VALID`, although it checks every write, so the planner can't use it to leave out a join.

AS IDENTITY`, all of which an inheritance parent keeps to itself, and `DROP TABLE` dropped every partition with no `CASCADE`. `ALTER TABLE ONLY` on the parent didn't stop them: it was refused with `column must be added to child tables too`, `constraint must be added to child tables too` and `inherited column ... must be renamed in child tables too`. > **A change that reaches a child or a partition needs every one declared.** On a partitioned table, or a table in old-style inheritance, Postgres carries most changes from the table to every child and partition: adding, dropping or renaming a column, `NOT NULL`, a default, a CHECK, and on a partitioned table also an index, a unique key, a foreign key, a trigger and identity. reqs.text: **What a child or a partition holds from its parent.** Postgres puts some of a parent's objects on each child and partition, and they belong to the parent. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, a CHECK on an inheritance parent or a partitioned table sat on every child, grandchild and partition under the parent's name, with `conislocal = false` and `coninhcount` counting the parents it came from, and a child of two parents held each one's. A foreign key, a primary key and a unique key on a partitioned table sat on every partition with `conparentid` pointing at the parent's constraint, `conislocal = false` and `coninhcount = 1`: the foreign key under the parent's name, the primary key as `<partition>_pkey`, the unique key under a name Postgres made, such as `q1_v_id_key`, and each under the partition's own name when `ATTACH PARTITION` took over a matching one the partition already had. An index on a partitioned table sat on every partition under a name Postgres made, such as `p1_a_idx`, or under the name of a matching index the partition had before `ATTACH PARTITION`, linked to the parent's index by a `pg_inherits` row whose `inhrelid` is the partition's index. A foreign key that references a partitioned table added a row on the referencing table for each partition, with `conparentid` set, named `r_x_fkey1` on 17.11 and `r_x_fkey_1` on 18.6. On 18.6 a `NOT NULL` is a `pg_constraint` row, and a child held its parent's under the parent's name, such as `parent_id_not_null`. An inheritance parent's foreign keys, primary key, unique keys and indexes weren't copied, and a CHECK marked `NO INHERIT` stayed on the parent. A child or a partition couldn't drop what it held, failing with `cannot drop inherited constraint` and `cannot drop index ... because index ... requires it`. `indisclustered` follows no tree: `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER ON` a partitioned table's index failed with `cannot mark index clustered in partitioned table`, and on a partition's index or an inheritance parent's index it marked that index alone. After `DETACH PARTITION`, everything the partition held became its own, with `conislocal = true`, `coninhcount = 0` and no `pg_inherits` row for its indexes, and after `NO INHERIT` a child's CHECKs became its own the same way. So the catalog reader reads each constraint with `coninhcount > 0` or `conparentid <> 0`, and each index with a parent index in `pg_inherits`, as part of the object it was copied from, which it reads once, on the table it was created on, and leaves it out of the child's, the partition's and the referencing table's own objects. A child's or a partition's model declares only its own constraints and indexes, the ones with `coninhcount = 0`, no `conparentid` and no parent index, and the parent's model declares the rest, once, apart from a partition's primary key, which R-1183 covers. Nullability stays a column's, read from `attnotnull` on every version, so Postgres 18's `NOT NULL` rows are never objects of their own. Postgres prints every index on a partitioned table with `ON ONLY`, as `CREATE INDEX p_a_ix ON ONLY x.p USING btree (a)` for one created without it, so the reader reads that definition as the same index on a plain table, which is how scratch builds it. A CHECK an inheritance child declares itself and also inherits, with `conislocal = true` and `coninhcount > 0`, is the parent's while it's inherited. When the parent's is dropped, Postgres keeps it on the child, with `coninhcount = 0`, as an object of the child's own that no model declares. reqs.text: **A partition's primary key.** Postgres names the key a partition holds from its partitioned table `<partition>_pkey`, which is morm's own name for a table's key. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `PARTITION OF`, and `ATTACH PARTITION` of a table with no key, built it as `<partition>_pkey` on the parent's key columns, in their order, with `conparentid` pointing at the parent's key and its index linked to the parent's in `pg_inherits`, and a partition of a partition held `<partition>_pkey` from its own parent's key. `ATTACH PARTITION` of a table that already had a key on those columns took it over under the name it had, such as `p2_pkey` or `p3_other`, and so did `ADD PRIMARY KEY` on a partitioned table whose partition already had one. When another relation already had the name, Postgres named the key `p5_pkey1`. A table can't hold two keys: `ADD PRIMARY KEY` on a partition that held its parent's failed with `multiple primary keys for table "p1" are not allowed`, and so did `ATTACH PARTITION` of a table whose key was on other columns. So a partition's model may declare `pk`, as the one exception to R-1174's rule that a child's or a partition's model declares only its own. The reader still reads the key as the parent's, one object, on the parent, and also records on each partition the key it holds, by name and columns. A partition's declared `pk` on the same columns, in the same order, under the name morm gives that table's key, is that key, not a second object, and a partition's model with no `pk` matches it too, as R-1174 says. A declared `pk` that differs from the key the partition holds, in its columns or its name, doesn't match it, as a key that differs on a plain table doesn't. So a key a partition holds on its parent's key columns under another name, such as `p3_other` or `p5_pkey1`, doesn't match a declared `pk`, and is drift on that partition until it's renamed `<partition>_pkey`. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, `ALTER TABLE p3 RENAME CONSTRAINT p3_other TO p3_pkey` renamed a key a partition held, and its index, keeping its `conparentid` and its index's `pg_inherits` row, under a brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the partition, and renaming `p5_pkey1` failed with `relation "p5_pkey" already exists` until the relation holding that name was renamed. An inheritance child holds no key from its parent, so its `pk` is its own, as on any table.

reqs.text: **A partition's `pk` in a migration.** Under step 29's rule for a partition's key, a partition's model with `pk` on the key it holds from its parent and one without it describe the same live table. So an op that adds that `pk` to a partition's model, or removes it, while the partition holds its parent's key on those columns under that name, changes nothing on the partition: preflight finds the op done, R-1168 doesn't refuse the removal as a drop of what the partition holds, which Postgres refuses with `cannot drop inherited constraint`, and its inverse in `rollback` and `down.sql` changes nothing either. When a migration adds a key to a partitioned table under `--fast`, as R-1160 says, and its partitions' models add `pk` on the same columns, the parent's `ADD PRIMARY KEY` builds each partition's key as `<partition>_pkey`, and each partition's op then finds it done, under R-1168's rule. A partition whose model already declares `pk` on those columns, with its own key under `<partition>_pkey`, keeps it: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11 the parent's `ADD PRIMARY KEY` took that key over, setting its `conparentid`, and the model's `pk` then matches the key the partition holds. A partition's `pk` that can't match its parent's key, before the migration or after it, such as one on other columns, one kept while the parent's key is dropped, or a partition's own key on other columns when the parent gets one, stops the run in preflight, as step 33 says.

reqs.text:
**A partition's `pk` that can't match its parent's key.** On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, dropping a partitioned table's key dropped the key every partition held from it, which a partition alone can't drop, failing with `cannot drop inherited constraint`, and dropping it and adding it on other columns, or in another order, built each partition's key again as `<partition>_pkey` on the new columns, a key held as `p3_other` included. `ADD PRIMARY KEY` on a partitioned table whose partition had a key of its own on other columns failed with `multiple primary keys for table "q2" are not allowed`. So a partition's declared `pk` that can't match the key it holds from its parent, under step 29's rule for a partition's key, would fail the gate or a step partway. `migrate` and `rollback` preflight read `pg_inherits`, `pg_class` and `pg_constraint` on the live database for every partition a model declares, and refuse with exit code `2` before the first step, changing nothing, naming the partition, the key its model declares, by its columns, and its parent's key, by name and columns, or saying the parent has none, in each of these cases, in the direction the run goes:

1. The partition's model declares `pk` on columns other than its parent's key's, or in another order, in the schema the run starts from, where the parent's key is the live one, or in the one it ends at, where it's the key the parent's model gives.
2. The migration drops its parent's key and the partition's model declares `pk` after it, on any columns, or changes the columns of its parent's key and the partition's model keeps `pk` on the old ones. Postgres drops the partition's key with the parent's, or builds it again on the new columns.
3. The migration gives its parent a key while the partition has a key of its own on other columns, whether its model declares it or not, and even when the same migration takes it out of the model, because Postgres refuses the parent's `ADD PRIMARY KEY` while it's there.

The message says how to go on: declare `pk` on the parent's key columns, in their order, or leave it out; in the migration that drops or changes the parent's key, take `pk` out of each partition's model, or change it the same way; and take a partition's own key on other columns out in an earlier migration than the one that gives its parent a key. A partition's model that changes `pk` the same way as its parent's, in the same migration, matches before and after it, under step 39's rule for a partition's `pk`. Where the parent has no key, before the migration and after it, a partition's `pk` is its own, compared as on any table. `makemigrations` can't see any of these, because the models don't say a table is a partition and scratch has none, so the first refusal comes when a command reaches the live database. `rehearse` runs this preflight too.

reqs.text: **Identity on a partition's model.** A partition takes its parent's identity, under step 29's rule for a partition's identity, and Postgres refuses identity of its own on a partition: `ATTACH PARTITION` of a table with an identity column, and adding identity to a partition's column, both fail. So `migrate` and `rollback` preflight refuse with exit code `2` before the first step, changing nothing, when a model declares identity on a column of a table that's a partition on the live database, in the schema the run starts from or the one it ends at, naming the partition, the column, and the parent's column whose identity it holds, or saying the parent's column has none.
