reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A partition's `pk` must stay on its parent's key.** A partition's model may mark `pk` on the key the partition holds from its partitioned table, on the parent's key columns, in their order. Postgres keeps that key in step with the parent's: dropping the parent's key drops every partition's, changing its columns builds every partition's again on the new ones, and adding a key to the parent fails while a partition has a key of its own on other columns. So `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before anything changes, naming the partition, the key its model marks and its parent's key, when a partition's model marks `pk` on other columns or in another order, when a migration drops or changes the parent's key and a partition's model keeps `pk` as it was, and when a migration gives the parent a key while a partition has its own on other columns. `makemigrations` can't see this, because your models don't say a table is a partition, so it shows up when a command reaches the database.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: otherwise the migration would fail partway, or leave a partition's key different from its model.
>
> **How to go on.** Mark `pk` on the parent's key columns, in their order, or leave it out. In the migration that drops or changes the parent's key, take `pk` out of each partition's model or change it the same way. Take a partition's own key on other columns out in an earlier migration than the one that gives the parent a key.
>
> **What you give up.** A partition can't keep a key of its own on other columns once its parent has one, and giving the parent a key can take one more migration.

reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the safe forms table:

> **A partition's model can't have identity, and the column its parent's identity fills is `db_set`.** A partition takes its values from its parent's identity, with no sequence of its own, and Postgres refuses identity of its own on a partition. `base = "common"` and `base = "pk_only"` add `id` as identity, and so does a field marked `identity`. So `migrate` and `rollback` stop with exit code `2` before anything changes when a partition's model has identity, naming the partition, the column and the parent's identity column. A partition's model whose inserts send the column its parent's identity fills is refused too, when a pool starts: under `GENERATED ALWAYS`, Postgres refuses every such insert with `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column`, and under `BY DEFAULT`, the keys you send can collide with the ones the parent's sequence gives later. So `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch`, naming the partition, the column and the parent's identity column, and saying to mark the field `db_set`. The compiler and `makemigrations` can't see either, because your models don't say a table is a partition, so they show up when a command or a pool reaches the database.
>
> **When it's right.** Always: Postgres would refuse the identity partway through the migration, and would refuse every insert that sends a `GENERATED ALWAYS` column.
>
> **How to go on.** Declare the partition's model with `base = "bare"`, mark `pk` on the parent's key columns, with no identity, and mark the column the parent's identity fills `db_set`, so inserts leave it out and Postgres gives each row the parent's next value, which the insert fills in on the row. When a migration adds identity to the parent's column, the partitions' models leave identity out and mark that column `db_set`, in the same release that marks the parent's column `identity`, deployed with the builds that insert into the table stopped, as the next notice says.
>
> **What you give up.** Inserts through a partition's model can't choose the key: each row gets the parent's next value. To write keys you choose, insert through the parent's model with `.explicit_ids()`, and Postgres puts each row in its partition.

reqs.text: **A partition's model that sends its parent's identity.** A partition's column that holds its parent's identity, under step 29's rule for a partition's identity, takes each value from the parent's sequence. Its model can't declare identity, as step 33's preflight says, so the field is a plain one that every insert sends, unless the model marks it `db_set`. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, on a partitioned table with `id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, `INSERT INTO p1 (id, k) VALUES (100, 1)` on its partition failed with `428C9` `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"`, while `INSERT INTO p1 (k) VALUES (1) RETURNING id` took `1` from the parent's sequence. Under `BY DEFAULT`, a sent `2` went in, and the sequence's second value then failed with `23505` on the partition's key. The partition's column showed the parent's `attidentity`, `a` or `d`, with no sequence of its own. So `check_schema`, at pool start as R-1116 says and in `db.check_schema()`, fails a model of a table that's a partition on the database, by `relispartition`, whose inserts send a column whose `attidentity` there is `a` or `d`, as one more insert case, under either kind: under `GENERATED ALWAYS` every insert through that model fails, and under `BY DEFAULT` the keys it sends can collide with ones the parent's sequence gives later. The finding names the partition, the column, the parent's identity column and its kind, and says to mark the field `db_set`, so inserts leave the column out and the row Postgres returns fills it. A `db_set` field there passes. It's read in R-1116's one statement, with no more round trips. R-1117's `check_schema = "off"` turns it off with the rest, and the README covers it beside the notice on a partition's identity.

reqs.text: **`rollback --fast` runs the down's one-transaction forms.** `--fast` means one thing on both sides: apps are stopped, so a step may run in its one-transaction form, under one lock, in place of a form built for live tables, as `makemigrations --fast` writes an up. reqs.text: **A model that sends a `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column.** A model's inserts send every field it doesn't mark `identity` or `db_set` and that isn't generated, through `insert`, `insert_many`, `upsert` and `insert_stream`, and an `Option` field counts, because an insert with a value sends it. Postgres refuses each such insert into a column with `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity, while `COPY` doesn't. On Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, after a plain `integer` key holding 1 and 2 got `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` with its sequence set to 2, `INSERT INTO t (id, v) VALUES (3, 'x')` failed with `428C9` `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"`, and so did one sending `NULL`, while one leaving `id` out took `3` and one with `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` stored its key. `COPY t (id, v)` stored a sent `3` with no error, and the next insert leaving `id` out was given `3` and failed with `23505`, on a plain table and on a partition. So `check_schema`, at pool start as R-1116 says and in `db.check_schema()`, fails a model of any table whose inserts send a column whose `attidentity` there is `a`, as one more insert case. The finding names the table and the column, says the column is `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity, which a build made before the migration that gave it identity doesn't know, and says to mark the field `db_set`, so inserts leave the column out and the row Postgres returns fills it, or `identity`, which leaves it out the same way and is what a model of a table morm migrates declares, so that the next `makemigrations` keeps the identity. A field marked `identity` or `db_set` passes, and `.explicit_ids()` never meets this, because it sends `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`. On a partition, that column gets R-1190's finding, naming the parent's identity column, and no second one. On a table that isn't a partition, a model that sends a column with `BY DEFAULT` identity passes, as before: its inserts go in, and the keys it sends can collide with the ones the sequence gives later, as R-1195 says. It's read in R-1116's one statement, from the `attidentity` that statement already reads for R-1190, with no more round trips. R-1117's `check_schema = "off"` turns it off with the rest, and the README covers it with its own notice.

reqs.text: **Adding identity in a rolling deploy.** A build made before a migration that adds identity to an existing column, by step 30's op, has a plain field on that column, which its inserts send. A build made with it marks the field `identity`, or `db_set` in a partition's model, as R-1190 says, so its inserts leave the column out. No order of model change, deploy and migration keeps both builds' inserts into that table working, and morm says so rather than offering one. With `migrate` first, from the moment the migration commits, every insert through the older build fails with `428C9` under `GENERATED ALWAYS`, and its `insert_stream` stores keys the sequence gives again later, failing an insert with `23505`. Under `BY DEFAULT` its inserts go in with the keys it chooses: on Postgres 18.6 and 17.11, after the migration set the sequence to 2, a sent `3` went in, and the next insert that left the column out was given `3` and failed with `23505`. With the new build first, the column is still `NOT NULL` with no default, so each insert leaving it out fails with `23502`, and R-0612's case for a column that has lost its default refuses that build at pool start. Reads, deletes and updates that don't set the column keep working in either order. So such a migration runs with every build that inserts into that table stopped, or with those inserts stopped: stop them, run `migrate`, then start the build made with the migration. reqs.text:
The README shows this notice loudly, beside the rolling deploy rows:

> **A build whose inserts send a `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column won't start.** Postgres refuses every insert that sends a value into a `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column, even `NULL`, with `cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column`. A field your model marks `identity` or `db_set` is left out of every insert, and `.explicit_ids()` adds the `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE` that lets your keys in. Any other field is sent, an `Option` one whenever it holds a value. So when a pool starts, `Db::connect()` returns `Error::SchemaMismatch` for a model, on any table, whose inserts send a column with `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity, naming the table and the column and saying to mark the field `db_set` or `identity`, before any of your queries run.
>
> **When it's right.** Always, for a build you mean to run. This is how a build made before a migration gave that column identity shows up, such as an older release brought back: it's refused at startup instead of failing each insert in production. It's worse with `insert_stream`: `COPY` stores the keys it sends with no error, and the sequence hands the same keys out again later, so a later insert fails with `duplicate key`. It also catches a newer build that took `identity` off a field before the migration that drops the identity has run.
>
> **How to go on.** Run the build made with the migration, whose model marks the field `identity`, or `db_set` in a partition's model. In a model of a table morm migrates, mark it `identity` rather than only `db_set`, so `makemigrations` keeps the identity. To write keys you choose, use `.explicit_ids()`. Plan the deploy that adds identity as the next paragraph says.
>
> **What you give up.** A build made before such a migration can't start again after it, so rolling the app back past it needs the migration rolled back too. A running one isn't stopped: morm checks once, when a pool starts, so its inserts into that table keep failing until you stop it. `check_schema = "off"` lets such a build start, and every insert it makes into that table fails. On a table that isn't a partition, a build that sends a `GENERATED BY DEFAULT` identity column still starts, and the keys it sends can collide with the ones the sequence gives later.

**Property tests:** random models and data round-trip through insert, read and JSON.
**Doc tests:** every README and doc example compiles and runs.
**`#[morm::test]`:** gives each test a database cloned from a migrated template, for this project and its users.
**Fault injection:** kill the process at every step boundary, then prove `--resume` and `rollback` both reach the right state.
**Property tests:** random schema A → B with data, including views, functions and triggers: up reaches B, down returns to A, preserved rows are intact.
**Op tests:** every op's inverse, with and without data
every dependency recreate path
**Concurrency:** rival migrators, migration under live traffic, lock-timeout retry.

**Retire:** deleting a parent succeeds after its child column is retired, rollback recreates the constraints, orphaned rows produce a decision, every recorded dependency from a live object refuses the retire, including `BEGIN ATOMIC` functions, `purge` never cascades and re-checks dependencies, and retires and renames named in a trigger function are caught, both managed and unmanaged, including a function in another schema that the table's triggers don't call, and a body that writes the names in another case, such as `SELECT N FROM T`.

**Safe forms:** `ADD PRIMARY KEY` on a nullable column takes no scan under lock, writes during a type-change copy aren't lost, the copy finishes under nonstop inserts, stopping at the highest key read once the trigger committed, long retired names don't collide, and `drop now` removes the data.
**Multi-step:** a fingerprint mismatch after the last step marks the migration `failed`.
**Forward only:** `rollback` and `rehearse` refused on production mode, the default on a new database, and `revert` restoring retired data.
**Squash:** a squashed chain gives the same schema as the full chain, and a database partway through is refused.

**Stale sessions:** a plpgsql trigger compiled before a hand-run swap fails with `XX000`, morm replaces the connection and the write succeeds once, other connections in the pool are replaced at checkout, and `pool_stats()` shows it. With a `BEGIN ATOMIC` function and a view under it dropped and recreated by hand in a loop, a caller that gets `XX000` with `could not open relation with OID` is retried once on the same connection and succeeds, on a pool and on a `db.hold()` connection, with nothing replaced and no generation raised. Inside a transaction it returns `Error::SchemaChanged`, and a retry that fails again returns its error.
**No false recovery:** a `42883` from SQL that was never cached isn't retried, a retried write applies once, and a cached statement that fails again returns its error.

**View above an online column swap:** on Postgres 15–18, with readers on the view and writers on the table through the swap, no read fails, no write is lost, and a prepared read recovers. Afterwards the view reads the new column and its new type and keeps its owner, comment and grants, `pg_depend` shows nothing on the retired column, and `purge` drops it with no `CASCADE`. A view over that view and a function over the view come through the same way, up, down and up, ending on the exact catalog. A view over a second table comes through with either table first in its `FROM`, and so do two views side by side, one with each table first, with readers on each view and on the second table, joins of the two tables in both orders, writers on both tables and transactions that write both in both orders: no deadlock, no failed read and no lost write. A reader arriving while the cutover holds its first lock gets its row, with no deadlock. A lock timeout leaves everything unchanged, and the cutover retries. A view no model declares, materialized or not, and a `SELECT *` view, materialized or not, are each refused with the full list before the swap's first step, changing nothing, and `--fast` handles the `SELECT *` views. **Retired materialized view:** on Postgres 15–18, after an online swap the old copy sits in `_morm_retired` with its rows, including a row the table has lost, and its indexes, owner, comment and grants, `verify` reports no drift, and a view beneath it is retired with it. `purge` drops the copy and what it reads before the retired column and type, with no `CASCADE`, and stops with the list if a live object depends on one. `rollback` restores it exactly, unpopulated if it was, with the new one gone, and `REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY` works on it afterwards. A type change on another column a retired copy reads exits with code `2` naming it, and runs after `purge --now`.

**Materialized view above an online column swap:** on Postgres 15–18, with readers on it, on a view over it and on the table, and writers on the table, a copy, an aggregate and a materialized view over another are built beside the old ones on the shadow column and swapped in a cutover of milliseconds. No read fails, no write is lost, and a prepared read recovers. Afterwards each reads the new column and its new type, matches the models and keeps its indexes, owner, comment and grants, with statistics. One over a managed view, and one over a `BEGIN ATOMIC` function, come through with what they read built beside them. A view and a function over it end on the new one, and only retired copies still read the retired column. Up, down and up ends on the exact catalog. The rebuild opens a decision, and no file is written until it's answered. A `WITH NO DATA` view stays unpopulated and opens none. **Live traffic, on Postgres 15–18:** an `integer` identity primary key on 1,000,000 rows, referenced by a `NOT NULL` column with `ON DELETE CASCADE` and a nullable one with `ON DELETE SET NULL`, each on 1,000,000 rows, widens to `bigint` under nonstop clients that insert a parent and two children, insert and then delete a parent, move a child to another parent, update a parent and then read its children, join, and run `SELECT *` on a referencing table, with more clients joining just before the cutover. No app transaction fails, every write count matches the clients' logs, no row is orphaned, no trigger or function is left, each copy stops at its bound, and the catalog equals a fresh build of the target schema, with the foreign keys tied to the new primary key and the sequence `bigint` at its position. The sequence keeps its options, owner, grants and comment, a `REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX` on the old key moves to the new one, and a session open across the cutover gets `55000` from `currval` until its next `nextval`. **Fault injection, on Postgres 15–18:** under the same traffic, kill the backend at every step boundary, and inside the copy, each concurrent index build, both `VALIDATE`s and the cutover. `--resume` then finishes with no lost write and the catalog of a fresh build, and `rollback --failed` drops every shadow object and leaves the old columns, keys and sequence working. A concurrent index left invalid is built again, a constraint left `NOT VALID` is validated again, and a cutover killed holding every lock changes nothing. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

**Up, down and up, on Postgres 15–18:** under live writers, a widening from `integer` to `bigint`, its `rollback` and the widening again each run online and end on the exact catalog, with the original columns back at their positions after the down and the identity's position carried each way. Once a key value or the sequence passes `2^31 - 1`, `rollback` is refused with exit code `2`, naming the table, the column and the value, with nothing changed, and a sequence that passes it after preflight stops the cutover with nothing changed. During the down, an insert of a value past `2^31 - 1` gets `22003`, and every write that fits succeeds. After `purge`, the down adds new shadow columns and still ends on the old types. With no writers, `rollback --fast` of the widening runs the down's `--fast` form, R-1126's one transaction, ends on the same catalog, and is refused the same way once a value doesn't fit. A migration that narrows `bigint` to `integer` runs in the same form. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

**One decision for the group, on Postgres 15–18:** with a managed function, a view and a trigger, each reaching a different column of the group, step 59's walk opens one decision listing what reaches every column of the group, the migration runs once it's answered, and the cutover refreshes those functions. An undeclared foreign key is refused, never offered as a decision.

**The cutover gives way, on Postgres 15–18:** under nonstop transactions that write a parent and then its children, children that check their parent, and readers joining them, no app transaction gets `40P01` or `55P03`, no read or write fails, and the cutover gets in by retrying, locking the key table first, and each new foreign key's step takes the referenced table's lock first. A group of 12 tables, where `cutover_lock_timeout` at `50ms` times its locks passes half the default `deadlock_timeout` of 1 s, runs with each lock waiting `deadlock_timeout / (2 × locks)`, the output saying so, and no app transaction killed. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

**Reverting a key widening, on Postgres 15–18:** on a database in production mode, `revert` of a migration that widened an `integer` identity primary key referenced by two tables to `bigint` writes a forward migration that runs online in step 60's form under live writers, with no failed app transaction and no lost write. It ends on the catalog the widening started from, apart from retired columns `purge` drops, with the original columns back at their positions and the identity's position carried. Once a key value or the sequence's position passes `2^31 - 1`, `migrate` of that forward migration is refused with exit code `2` before its first step, naming the table, the column and the value, with nothing changed.

`identity` on a `u64` field, and on a field whose `sql` is `numeric(20,0)`, `text` or `uuid`, each fail with a message naming the field and the three types identity allows, while `identity` on `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint`, `int4` and `int8` compiles

Plain `rollback` runs the default forms, with `NOT VALID` and `VALIDATE` in separate transactions and concurrent builds, and `rollback --fast` runs each `--fast` form in one transaction, ending on the same catalog and rows as the default forms. On Postgres 15 to 17, the `rollback` of a retire that adds back a foreign key from a partitioned table, which plain `rollback` refuses with exit code `2`, runs under `rollback --fast` and ends validated on every partition, and a unique key missing a partition-key column is refused under both. If a result contradicts this design, stop and ask the owner with the evidence and options.

**A model that sends a `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity column, on Postgres 15–18:** on a plain table whose `id` is `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, a binary whose model has `id` as a plain `i32` field, and one whose model has it as an `Option<i32>` field, each get `Error::SchemaMismatch` from `Db::connect()`, before any of the app's statements has run, with a finding naming the table and `id`, saying it's `GENERATED ALWAYS` identity and saying to mark the field `db_set` or `identity`. With `check_schema = "off"` that binary connects, `db.check_schema()` returns the same finding, an `insert` sending `id` gets `428C9`, and an `insert_stream` sending the key the sequence gives next stores it with no error, after which an `insert` through a binary that marks `id` `identity` fails with `23505` on that key. A binary whose model marks `id` `identity`, and one whose model marks it `db_set`, each connect, their inserts leave `id` out and get the sequence's next values, filled on the returned rows, and `.explicit_ids()` stores a chosen `id`. A binary whose model takes `identity` off `id` before a migration that drops the identity has run gets the same finding. On a partitioned table with `id` `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, a partition's model that sends `id` gets one finding for it, R-1190's, naming the parent's identity column. On a plain table whose `id` is `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY`, a model that sends `id` connects. With every finding above in one binary, the pool's first connection sends one statement for the check, as `log_statement = 'all'` shows.

**Adding identity in a rolling deploy, on Postgres 15–18:** on a plain table whose `NOT NULL` `integer` `id` holds rows, with a binary built before the migration running with a plain `id` field, `makemigrations` from a model that marks `id` `identity`, once `GENERATED ALWAYS` and once `BY DEFAULT`, writes the op in `expand`, exits as it would with no warning, and prints a warning naming the table, `id` and the kind, saying that no deploy order avoids it and to stop the builds that insert into that table before `migrate`, in `--json` too. Before the migration, the binary built with it gets `Error::SchemaMismatch` from `Db::connect()`, naming `id` as a column that has lost its default. `migrate --plan` and `migrate` print the same warning, and `migrate` runs. Afterwards, under `GENERATED ALWAYS`, the running older binary's inserts get `428C9` while its reads, its updates of other columns and its deletes work, and restarted it gets R-1194's finding. Under `BY DEFAULT`, the older binary's insert of the next key goes in, and the next insert through the new binary fails with `23505` on it. The new binary connects, and its inserts get keys past the highest the table held. `rollback` prints the same warning, and afterwards the new binary's inserts get `23502` and the older binary's inserts work. On a partitioned table whose `id` gets identity the same way, the release whose partition models mark `id` `db_set` gets `Error::SchemaMismatch` before the migration and connects after it, while partition models built before it get R-1190's finding at restart. A migration that adds a column with identity, one that creates a table with it, and one that changes `id` from `BY DEFAULT` to `GENERATED ALWAYS` on a column every model marks `identity` print no warning, and a binary built before each keeps inserting through it, `.explicit_ids()` included.
